title: What the Optimizely incident reveals about third-party website scripts
text:
November 18, 2026

|

Security intelligence

What the Optimizely incident reveals about third-party website scripts

By Field Effect Security Intelligence Team

On November 17, 2026, Optimizely, a software company that provides tools for building and optimizing websites, disclosed that a threat actor exploited a vulnerability in its Web Experimentation platform and injected malicious JavaScript into customer projects. Optimizely's Web Experimentation product allows organizations to test different versions of web pages, such as alternate checkout layouts, to determine which performs better for visitors.
Initial reporting focused on Optimizely. On November 16, 2026, compromised Optimizely snippets delivered malicious code to visitors of customer websites. Researchers found the injected code in 188 of the 1,611 Optimizely snippets they examined, affecting 178 organizations.
Researchers later identified tampered scripts associated with three additional web services, Kissmetrics, StorifyMe, and Minute Media, that may have used the same infrastructure. The earliest observed activity involving those services dates to November 13, 2026, three days before the Optimizely injections.
The malicious code performed several functions, including:

Replacing cryptocurrency wallet addresses

Capturing payment card data entered into checkout forms

Collecting cookies and page screenshots

Redirecting iPhone and iPad users to infrastructure associated with iOS exploit kits

Optimizely has since fixed the vulnerability and removed the malicious code from affected projects. How the code reached the other three services has not been publicly disclosed.
Since these reports emerged, we have received questions from partners and clients about whether Field Effect MDR would detect this activity.
In this campaign, the affected organizations’ own servers, networks, and website code remained unchanged. Instead, the threat actor altered code hosted on third-party vendor platforms, which was then executed within visitors’ web browsers.
Because both the compromise and the resulting data theft occurred outside environments typically monitored by MDR services, activity of this type generally falls outside MDR visibility and into the domain of web fraud investigations, payment processors, and incident response activities focused on customer-facing web applications.
Keep reading to learn how the attack worked, who may be affected, what organizations can do to determine whether their websites loaded compromised scripts, and where traditional security monitoring provides visibility.
What is Optimizely Web Experimentation?
Optimizely is a digital experience platform. Its Web Experimentation product enables marketing and e-commerce teams to run A/B tests and personalize website content. Organizations deploy the service by loading a JavaScript snippet, typically from Optimizely’s content delivery network (CDN) at cdn.optimizely[.]com, although some organizations serve the same snippet from their own domains.
Optimizely generates each snippet from a customer’s project configuration and automatically republishes it whenever project settings change. As a result, changes made within the Optimizely platform can immediately affect website visitors without requiring any modification to the website itself.
One configuration option, the Project JavaScript field, allows custom code to execute on every page that loads the Optimizely snippet. Anyone who gains the ability to modify that field can effectively run code in the browser of every visitor to every affected page.
Because the Optimizely snippet is often added by marketing teams or through tag management platforms such as Google Tag Manager, security and IT teams may be unaware that it is present.
How do third-party scripts work?
Website owners add third-party scripts to get features without building them: testing tools such as Optimizely, analytics that count and track visitors, chat windows, video players and […]

title: Apache Axis exploitation highlights legacy component risks
text:
November 18, 2026

|

Security intelligence

Apache Axis exploitation highlights legacy component risks

By Field Effect Security Intelligence Team

At a glance:

CVE-2026-90436 is a critical unauthenticated remote code execution vulnerability in Apache Axis 1.x, an end-of-life framework embedded in multiple products and custom Java applications.

Exploitation was reported shortly after public proof-of-concept code became available on November 12, 2026.

Apache Axis 1.x is frequently bundled inside larger applications, making vulnerable deployments difficult to identify, inventory, and track.

Threat summary
On November 16, 2026, researchers reported active exploitation of CVE-2026-90436, a critical remote code execution vulnerability affecting Apache Axis 1.x. Exploitation began within hours of a public proof-of-concept (POC) release, and threat actors targeted software that embeds the vulnerable framework: Atlassian Confluence Data Center and N-able N-central.
Apache Axis 1.x is an end-of-life Simple Object Access Protocol (SOAP) web services framework developed by the Apache Software Foundation. Before REST APIs became the dominant integration method, SOAP web services connected enterprise applications, management platforms, identity services, and business software.
Axis received SOAP requests, processed Extensible Markup Language (XML) messages, and invoked application functions remotely. Although it is no longer maintained, Apache Axis 1.x remains embedded in some commercial products and custom Java applications.
CVE-2026-90436 lies in how Axis processes inbound SOAP fault messages. During processing, Axis can instantiate a Java class referenced in a specially crafted request before validating whether that class is safe to load.
If a suitable class exists on the target system, arbitrary code execution can occur. The vulnerability is remotely exploitable, requires no authentication or user interaction, and can be triggered whenever a vulnerable SOAP service is reachable over the network.
CISA assigned a CVSS v3.1 score of 9.8, and Atlassian assigned a CVSS v4 score of 9.3 for affected Confluence deployments.
Because the Axis project is no longer supported, remediation falls to downstream vendors and to organizations that still operate Axis-based applications. In the cases observed so far, Confluence and N-central exposed Axis through legacy SOAP-based APIs. When those interfaces were enabled and reachable, an attacker could send a crafted SOAP request and achieve code execution before authentication.
In some cases, exploitation was chained with additional vulnerabilities to obtain elevated privileges. Potential impact depends on the affected application but can include arbitrary command execution, credential theft, malware deployment, access to connected systems, or compromise of administration platforms.
Analysis
Axis 1.x ships as a Java library that runs embedded inside other applications. Most software inventories track products rather than embedded libraries, so organizations may be unaware they run it. Vendors incorporated it years ago, and it remained in place after support ended.
As of November 17, 2026, Confluence and N-central are the only commercial products publicly confirmed as affected, but exposure extends further.
Apache Axis can run as a standalone web application, be embedded in internally developed Java software, be packaged as a dependency in enterprise applications, or be installed from operating system repositories.
The Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) record lists the Maven packages axis:axis and org.apache.axis:axis through version 1.4 as affected. Ubuntu and Debian track their Axis packages as affected with no fixed version available.
Standalone deployments expose the vulnerable code path whenever a SOAP endpoint is reachable, and there is no legacy API setting to switch off. Service-level authentication offers no protection, because Axis processes the malicious fault message before […]

title: Java4Shell raises broad enterprise Java exposure concerns
text:
November 18, 2026

|

Security intelligence

Java4Shell raises broad enterprise Java exposure concerns

By Field Effect Security Intelligence Team

At a glance:

CVE-2026-114938, informally known as "Java4Shell," is a critical memory corruption vulnerability affecting the Base64 decoder in the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM). Specially crafted Base64 input may cause a JVM crash and could enable unauthenticated remote code execution.

The vulnerability has received significant attention because it affects a core Java runtime component that may be present across numerous enterprise applications, identity platforms, development tools, and commercial software products.

CISA has urged organizations to identify affected Java deployments and apply vendor updates immediately, prioritizing internet-facing systems.

Threat summary
On November 17, 2026, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) issued an alert urging organizations to immediately patch CVE-2026-114938, a critical vulnerability dubbed "Java4Shell." The vulnerability affects the Base64 decoder within the x86-64 HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM), a core component of many Java Runtime Environment (JRE) and Java Development Kit (JDK) deployments. Specially crafted Base64 input can reportedly trigger memory corruption that may result in unauthenticated remote code execution.
The vulnerability has generated widespread concern because it affects the Java runtime rather than a single vendor application. OpenJDK, the open-source reference implementation of Java SE, serves as the code base for Oracle JDK, Eclipse Temurin, Amazon Corretto, Azul Zulu, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Red Hat Build of OpenJDK, SAP Machine, BellSoft Liberica, and many Linux OpenJDK packages. Many commercial applications, appliances, and container images also bundle their own Java runtime, making affected deployments difficult to identify through traditional asset inventories.
Base64 encoding is widely used in authentication headers, application programming interface (API) requests, authentication tokens, and application integrations. Applications commonly decode this data before processing credentials, tokens, or other user-supplied input. Researchers identified examples where the affected decoder can be reached through HTTP Basic authentication and JSON Web Token (JWT) processing workflows, allowing attacker-controlled data to reach the vulnerable code path before credentials or signatures are validated.
The vulnerability is an integer underflow that causes an out-of-bounds write on the Java heap. A malformed Base64 string ending with an equals sign can cause the decoder to write 62 or 63 bytes beyond the end of the output array. Confirmed vulnerability behavior consists of heap corruption and JVM instability resulting from the memory corruption condition.
Researcher demonstrations showed that the memory corruption can be leveraged to achieve remote code execution. The vulnerability has been assigned a CVSS v4 score of 9.2. Although exploitation is remote, unauthenticated, and requires no user interaction, exposure is limited to systems that meet three specific conditions.
1. The system must be running an affected Java release
The vulnerable code was introduced in OpenJDK 17.0.6 and is present in later Java 17 releases and all feature releases beginning with Java 18, including Java 21, Java 25, and Java 27. Java 8, Java 11, and Java 17.0.5 and earlier do not contain the vulnerable implementation. 
2. The system must be running on supported hardware
The vulnerable code path is an optimized HotSpot decoding routine that uses Advanced Vector Extensions 512 (AVX-512) Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions (VBMI) and AVX-512 Byte and Word (BW) instructions on supported x86-64 processors. Systems that do not support these instruction sets use a different decoding implementation and do not execute the vulnerable code. 
3. Attacker-controlled Base64 data must reach the affected […]

title: The forced audit: how AuditTeam’s OpsAgent framework masks ransomware as consulting
text:
BackgroundTechnical detailsLoadersOpsAgent main implantCommands descriptionAdditional modulesAV/EDR killer moduleCryptor moduleOpsAgent-rs (Rust version)InfrastructureVictimsAttributionConclusionsIndicators of compromiseFile hashesFile paths

Authors

Vladimir Nestor

AuditTeam is an active threat group that uses the OpsAgent framework to compromise organizations across at least seven countries and territories. The campaign began in January 2026 and remained active through October 2026, at a minimum. In its ransom note, AuditTeam demands an “Audit & Consulting fee” in exchange for vulnerability reports. During this period, the group has infected dozens of organizations in Russia, Italy, the Philippines, Hong Kong, Senegal, Finland and China. The group’s leak site also claims victims in seven additional countries.
OpsAgent provides file system management, process injection, privilege escalation, keylogging, screenshot capture, and network pivoting. During the campaign OpsAgent was transitioned from C++ to Rust while adding new capabilities including interactive shells and WebSocket upgrades. Its command-and-control domains use Amazon CloudFront subdomains, which OpsAgent discovers via a public GitHub repository. Two specialized modules extend its functionality. An antivirus/endpoint detection and response (AV/EDR) killer module installs a digitally signed Beijing Jiangmin Antivirus driver to terminate security products. A cryptor module encrypts files using AES-CBC or ChaCha20 with X25519 key exchange and targets database processes for termination prior to doing so.
Background
On March 10, 2026, we discovered suspicious activity targeting an organization in Hong Kong. The tool used was OpsAgent, a framework designed to resemble a penetration testing utility. Further investigation revealed attacks in additional countries, prompting an active research phase. This implant offers extensive operator capabilities, including host reconnaissance, shellcode injection via named pipes, and lateral movement through agent networks based on compromised hosts.
Analysis indicates OpsAgent was used by AuditTeam. The group was first mentioned publicly by dbdigest.com in March 2026. On June 25, 2026, DeXpose reported that AuditTeam had claimed responsibility for an attack on a Russian organization and listed it on its leak site. AuditTeam leaves a ransom note threatening to release stolen data unless a fee is paid. They call this fee the “Audit & Consulting fee.” According to the note, payment results in a vulnerability report being delivered to the victim instead of leaking the stolen data archive to the public internet. While the note does not mention file encryption, it is left by the cryptor module. Therefore, if a victim sees the note, their files are already encrypted.
The ransom note
GitHub commit history shows the campaign started on January 5, 2026. The leak site lists its first victim on February 21, 2026. Dozens of machines across at least seven countries were infected. On August 19, 2026, a C2 domain for the new OpsAgent version was added to the public repository and subsequently used in attacks.
AuditTeam activity timeline
Technical details
Loaders
OpsAgent uses multiple loader variants during its campaign. All discovered loaders unpack OpsAgent by parsing the MZ header and transferring execution to the entry point of the unpacked payload.
The C loader was discovered in April 2026. It injects shellcode into msiexec.exe using standard API calls: CreateProcessA, VirtualAllocEx, WriteProcessMemory, and CreateRemoteThread.
The .NET loader was found in June 2026. It uses NtQueueApcThread instead of direct process creation for injection. It contains strings such as DApc, DProtect, DResume, and msiexec.exe. Both the C and .NET loaders inject shellcode into a separate target process. They are also protected by OLLVM obfuscation with control-flow flattening enabled.

APACHE ROLLER RCE FLAW CVE-2026-129448 UNDER ACTIVE ATTACK
Pierluigi Paganini

November 18, 2026
Attackers are exploiting a critical Apache Roller flaw that allows unauthenticated remote code execution, prompting urgent security updates.

A critical vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-129448 (CVSS score of 9.8), in Apache Roller could allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary code on a vulnerable server. Apache Roller is an open-source blogging platform written in Java. According to the Apache Software Foundation (ASF) the flaw is being actively exploited in attacks in the wild.

The issue affects Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4. It stems from unsafe deserialization in the platform’s XML-RPC endpoint, which processes certain data before checking whether the requester is authenticated. An attacker doesn’t need valid credentials to reach this vulnerable code path.

“Deserialization of Untrusted Data in Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code. The XML-RPC endpoint accepts vendor extension types and deserializes them before authenticating the requester.” reads the security notice published on the Apache mailing list. “This is the same vulnerability as CVE-2026-82384, which listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected.”

The Apache project described the problem in its security notice published on the Apache mailing list:

The maintainers explained that the XML-RPC endpoint accepts vendor extension types and deserializes them before authenticating the requester. This order of operations is the core security problem: the application processes attacker-controlled data before establishing whether the request should be trusted.

The ASF also confirmed that the vulnerability is the same issue previously tracked as CVE-2026-82384. That earlier advisory, published in September 2026, listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected. The new notice expands the affected version range to include releases from 4.0.0 through 6.1.4, […]

NORWEGIAN GAS GIANT EQUINOR SAYS IT’S UNDER CYBERATTACK. PRODUCTION KEEPS RUNNING
Pierluigi Paganini

November 18, 2026
Norwegian Gas Giant Equinor confirms cyberattack on IT systems, with no impact on production or confirmed data theft.

Equinor, Europe’s largest gas supplier, said on 17 November it had detected an ongoing cyberattack against some IT systems. The Norwegian company said the attack had not affected operations and production, and it had taken steps to neutralise it.

“Equinor has detected an ongoing cyber-attack against certain IT systems. Relevant resources have been mobilised to neutralise the attack and regain full integrity.” reads the statement published by the company. “As this is not a virus attack, there is no risk of the attack spreading. At present, there is no indication that the attack has consequences for employees, partners or suppliers. Production remains unaffected.”

The energy giant said there was also no indication data had been stolen. A company spokesperson declined to give further details.

The disruption reached everyday work, not the wells. Norwegian news agency NTB reported, citing the company, that IT applications and internal systems were affected, and a person at Equinor told Reuters the internal email system was down.

Norway’s National Security Authority (NSM) said it was aware of the attack and was ready to provide support if needed. Last month, the agency raised its cyber threat level to four on a five-level scale. It warned that cyberattacks could disrupt critical services such as water and electricity. NSM also reported that successful cyberattacks against Norwegian companies had tripled in the previous six months.

“The incident currently being ⁠experienced ​by Equinor confirms that this risk ​is indeed high,” the NSM spokesperson said on Tuesday.

65 CHARACTERS TO RCE: INSIDE THE JAVA4SHELL VULNERABILITY
Pierluigi Paganini

November 18, 2026
Calif disclosed Java4Shell, a critical OpenJDK Base64 bug enabling pre-auth RCE in Jenkins, Jira, Keycloak and more. Patches are out. Update now.

Calif researchers disclosed Java4Shell, a memory-corruption bug, tracked as CVE-2026-114938 (CVSS score of 9.2), in OpenJDK’s Base64 decoder. OpenJDK is the world’s most common Java runtime. OpenJDK (Open Java Development Kit) is the open-source implementation of the Java platform. It provides the tools and components needed to develop and run Java applications, including the Java Virtual Machine (JVM), libraries and development tools. It is widely used in enterprise systems, servers and cloud environments.

Base64 shows up everywhere: authentication, file uploads, network messages. To decode it fast, OpenJDK uses special x86-64 instructions that process many bytes at once, and the bug lives in that hand-written machine code. A single malformed string triggers it: 64 “A” characters followed by one equals sign, or 128 on older OpenJDK 17.

The flaw sits in how the decoder handles padding at the end of a Base64 string. When the trailing characters are “=”, “==” or similar, the code can compute a negative output length, and that underflow turns into a write of all 64 bytes instead of the few that should go out. For a 65-character trigger, OpenJDK allocates a 50-byte buffer and ends up writing 62 bytes past its end.

“At runtime, the decoded buffer length is calculated as (ceil(inp_len / 4) * 3) - padding. When the bug is triggered, with 65 bytes ([64 bytes] + '=') as input, that calculation allocates a 50-byte buffer. During decoding the bug makes output_mask == -1 for evmovdqub, so 64 bytes are written starting at offset 48, an out-of-bounds write past the end of the buffer.” reads the report published by Calif. “On OpenJDK 17, the trigger input is 'A' * 128 + '=' instead of 'A' * 64 + '=', because the length threshold to reach the code path is higher.”

U.S. CISA ADDS PERFORCE PUPPET ENTERPRISE FLAW TO ITS KNOWN EXPLOITED VULNERABILITIES CATALOG
Pierluigi Paganini

November 18, 2026
U.S. CISA adds Perforce Puppet Enterprise vulnerability CVE-2026-115731 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added a Perforce Puppet Enterprise flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-115731 (CVSS score of 9.4), to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog.

The critical vulnerability CVE-2026-115731 affects Puppet Server and could allow an attacker to execute arbitrary code remotely on a vulnerable server. The flaw is caused by improper deserialization of untrusted data in Puppet’s report-processing component.

The vulnerability can be exploited by a client holding a certificate signed by the Puppet Certificate Authority (CA). An attacker can send a specially crafted report through an HTTP PUT request to trigger the flaw and execute code with the privileges of the Puppet Server service account. This could give the attacker control over the server and potentially provide a path to compromise systems managed by the Puppet infrastructure.

The risk is even greater when the CA automatically signs certificate requests without properly verifying them. In this configuration, an attacker with network access may be able to obtain a valid agent certificate without prior authentication and then exploit the vulnerability.

As of the latest available vendor information, there are no reports confirming active exploitation of CVE-2026-115731. Perforce has stated that it is not aware of attacks exploiting the flaw and has found no evidence of customer data being accessed. No specific threat actor or campaign has been linked to this vulnerability.

Perforce released security updates on November 3, 2026. Fixed versions include Puppet Enterprise 2026.0.1, 2025.12.1 and 2023.8.13, and Puppet Core 9.1.3 and 8.22.2. Organizations should upgrade as soon as possible. Until then, they should […]

title: Java4Shell: Critical OpenJDK Flaw Allows Unauthenticated Remote Code Execution
text: Key findingsCVE-2026-114938, which has been dubbed Java4Shell, is a critical heap overflow in the Base64 decoder of the OpenJDK HotSpot Java Virtual Machine (JVM) on x86-64. It has a Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) v4.0 score of 9.2 (Critical), according to Calif, which discovered the flaw, and 8.1 (High) on CVSS 3.1 per OpenJDK's advisory.A remote, unauthenticated attacker who can deliver crafted Base64 input to a vulnerable Java process can corrupt heap memory and achieve remote code execution (RCE). No user interaction is required for server-side attacks.Only hosts with AVX-512 Vector Byte Manipulation Instructions (VBMI) are exposed. That means Intel Ice Lake or newer, or AMD Zen 4 or newer. ARM64 hosts, Java 11 and standard OpenJDK 8 are not affected.Security company Calif demonstrated pre-authentication RCE in test configurations of Keycloak, Jira, Confluence, Artifactory, Jenkins and PingFederate.Oracle and OpenJDK released fixes on November 17, 2026. Fixed builds end in ".1", and the same version number without the suffix remains vulnerable.No in-the-wild exploitation had been reported as of publication, but a proof-of-concept trigger is public. Symantec and Carbon Black Security Response is investigating, and up-to-date protection information will be added to our Protection Bulletin.OverviewA critical vulnerability in OpenJDK, CVE-2026-114938 (aka Java4Shell), was disclosed on November 17, 2026. The flaw sits in the optimized Base64 decoder that the HotSpot JVM uses on x86-64 processors with AVX-512 VBMI support. Oracle and OpenJDK have released patches, and the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) urged immediate patching. At time of writing on November 18 there has been no evidence found of in-the-wild exploitation of this bug.Java4Shell is significant because Base64 decoding is routine in server software. Authentication headers, JSON Web Tokens (JWT), Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) assertions, file uploads and API fields are all Base64 encoded, so internet-facing login and API services decode attacker-controlled data by design. Calif, the security firm that first reported the flaw, published a standalone trigger and said product-specific exploit chains would be held back until upgrades are more widespread. Details about the flaw became public before patches were available.How the vulnerability worksThe store mask used by the decoder is wrong when the Base64 input ends in padding. As a result, the calculated output length underflows, and the decoder writes a full 64 bytes into a buffer that is smaller than that. According to Calif, a 65-byte input overflows the heap by 62 bytes, which corrupts adjacent Java objects, allowing an actor to gain heap read and write primitives, which makes the bug remotely exploitable.Exploitation of the heap overflow depends on the layout of the target application, and a failed attempt can crash the JVM. A crash would result in denial of service, but Calif reported that retries often succeed. Heap memory disclosure is also possible. A client-side variant exists: a Java application that connects over Transport Layer Security (TLS) to a malicious server can be compromised.Who is affected?Affected versions are OpenJDK 17.0.6 and later (including 17.0.6 to 17.0.21), Java 21 before 21.0.13.1, Java 25 before 25.0.5.1 and Java 27. Oracle also lists Java SE 8 8u511b33-perf. Builds from Oracle, Corretto, Temurin, Microsoft, Zulu, Liberica, SapMachine, Red Hat and GraalVM are affected. Hosts must also run on an x86-64 processor with AVX-512 VBMI, which includes Intel Ice Lake and newer and AMD Zen 4 and newer. Java 11, standard OpenJDK 8, ARM64 hosts and x86 processors without AVX-512 VBMI are not affected.Enterprise and server deployments carry the most risk, particularly identity, application lifecycle, build pipeline, artifact and data platforms. Popular Java-based applications such as Jira, Confluence, Jenkins, Keycloak, Kafka and Elasticsearch […]

title: Behind the Power Outage: Unmasking a New Intrusion Vector in Enterprise Infrastructure Tools
text: Key findings Symantec's Threat Intelligence and Research Team analyzed an intrusion in which the attacker used CyberPower PowerPanel Business (PPB), a software that manages UPS devices, as their execution channel on a Windows domain controller. PPB can run a script (a .cmd file in an extcmd folder) when a power-related event such as a voltage sag or outage is detected. The attacker placed their own scripts in that folder through the product's web console and had the PowerPanel service, ppbed.exe, run them. The commands in this attack chain have ppbed.exe as their ancestor and run as SYSTEM. The PPB web service receives requests to its /local/rest/v1/file/upload endpoint on TCP port 3052. The attacker used this channel to download tools with certutil, then loaded a .NET assembly into memory using PowerShell, and ran ntdsutil and esentutl against the Active Directory database, ntds.dit.  The attackers iterated the scripts, step-by-step, until the collection process worked successfully. The attacker then used the same channel to launch a long-running implant, upnpcont.exe, which loads a malicious atl.dll. Its process tree leads back to ppbed.exe. Public advisories document issues including hard-coded credentials, a default administrator password, and a file-upload path-traversal flaw in PPB. Any of these, or stolen administrator credentials, could give an attacker the necessary console access to carry out the attack described in this blog. Attackers have long favored using legitimate tools to help them carry out malicious activities on compromised systems. Using such tools allows them to hide in plain sight by making their activities appear to originate from legitimate and trusted sources. This reduces the risk of detection when trying to deploy additional components, which may result in files getting blocked during installation and raising alarms. Common tools such as backup solutions like Veeam, and remote monitoring management (RMM) tools such as AnyDesk and ScreenConnect are frequently abused by attackers to enable remote command execution and control during breaches. While these tools dominate the headlines, new tools that can be abused are constantly found by attackers to offer the functionality they require.  The latest example is CyberPower’s PowerPanel Business edition, an application for managing CyberPower’s line of UPS devices, aimed at the small-to-medium businesses (SMBs) segment. It is used to manage critical systems that require a graceful shutdown in the event of a power fault.  Why CyberPower PowerPanel Business is an attractive target PPB is usually installed on critical machines that must be shut down cleanly, even during a power failure. These include machines running hypervisors, database servers, file servers, and, in this case, domain controllers (DCs). These also happen to be the systems that an intruder most wants to control. Machines running PPB typically share three properties that make them useful to an attacker: Built-in command execution. The vendor's documentation describes an event-action setting in which an administrator selects a command file, saved with a .cmd extension in the extcmd folder of the installation directory. When the event fires, the service runs the provided script. Scripts can be provided with data through variables such as %EVENT% and %MODULE_NO%. A network-facing management interface. The web management console is served by an embedded Tomcat server on TCP port 3052 and has a REST API. Uploaded files pass through Tomcat's work directory under the product's web-server\work\tomcat\localhost\local folder. A privileged, trusted service. The service, ppbed.exe starts under services.exe and runs as S-1-5-18 (SYSTEM). Commands launched through it inherit that identity. For an attacker to abuse PPB for malicious purposes, no complicated memory-corruption exploit, and no new service or scheduled task is necessary. In process telemetry, the activity looks like a power-management product […]

CVE-2026-114938: Java4Shell Flaw Enables Pre-Auth RCE in Major Java Applications
text:
En

CVEs

November 18, 2026
8 min read

A newly disclosed vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-114938 and dubbed Java4Shell exposes certain Java environments to memory corruption, sensitive data disclosure, service crashes, and potentially remote code execution. The flaw resides in OpenJDK’s hardware-accelerated Base64 decoder and can be triggered remotely when attacker-controlled Base64 data reaches the vulnerable Java runtime.

Calif researchers demonstrated pre-authentication RCE against widely deployed enterprise applications running default configurations, including Keycloak, Atlassian Jira, Atlassian Confluence, JFrog Artifactory, Jenkins, and PingFederate. Authenticated exploitation was also demonstrated against Apache Kafka Broker, Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, Gerrit, and Spinnaker, while sample Spring Boot and Apache Struts applications were successfully exploited as well.

The vulnerability is highly dependent on the underlying hardware. The vulnerable accelerated decoder runs on x86-64 processors supporting AVX-512 VBMI, including Intel Xeon Ice Lake and newer server platforms and AMD Zen 4 or later systems. ARM64 systems are not known to be affected by this specific flaw.

Calif assigned Java4Shell a CVSS 4.0 score of 9.2, Critical, while Oracle rates it 8.1, High under CVSS 3.1. Oracle released security updates on November 17, 2026, while several downstream Java vendors have been issuing their own patched builds on separate schedules.

Organizations can leverage SOC Prime’s AI-Native Detection Intelligence Platform to accelerate threat hunting and detection engineering around emerging vulnerabilities and adapt relevant detection logic across SIEM, EDR, XDR, and Data Lake environments.

Security teams can also use Prime Architect to transform emerging vulnerability intelligence into hunting queries, refine detection logic, and adapt behavioral detections to the telemetry available within their infrastructure.

CVE-2026-114938 analysis

CVE-2026-114938 affects OpenJDK 17 beginning with version 17.0.6 and subsequent Java 17 builds, as well as affected Java 21, 25, and 27 releases derived from the vulnerable OpenJDK code. Multiple downstream distributions inherit the issue, including Oracle Java SE, Amazon Corretto, Eclipse Temurin, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK, Azul Zulu, BellSoft Liberica, SAP SapMachine, and Red Hat OpenJDK. Standard Java 8 and Java 11 do not contain the vulnerable code path, although Oracle’s Java SE 8 Performance Pack build 8u511b33-perf is specifically listed as affected.

The vulnerability originates in the optimized implementation of java.util.Base64.Decoder. On supported x86-64 CPUs, the JVM can automatically select AVX-512 VBMI accelerated instructions on supported x86-64 processors to improve Base64 decoding performance. Specially malformed Base64 input causes the decoder to miscalculate the amount of data that should be written to the destination buffer, resulting in a heap-based out-of-bounds write.

According to Calif’s technical analysis, one malformed input pattern causes the accelerated routine to write approximately 62 bytes beyond the allocated output buffer. Java ultimately rejects the malformed Base64 value, but the memory corruption occurs before the validation failure stops processing.

This behavior is particularly dangerous because Base64 decoding occurs throughout enterprise Java applications. HTTP Basic authentication headers, SAML artifacts, CSRF tokens, encoded file uploads, MIME content, and other application data may all pass through the standard Java decoder. Importantly, many of these operations can take place before a user is authenticated, creating pathways toward pre-authentication exploitation.

Researchers initially faced an important limitation: the bytes written beyond the buffer are largely fixed rather than freely attacker-controlled. Calif developed an application-dependent exploitation technique that manipulates the JVM heap layout so the overflow corrupts […]

title: React2STEAL Uses GitHub Actions to Exploit React2Shell
text: Jump to sectionEarlier today, I got a message from Karina Reaño, a Cyber Threat Intelligence Lead. She'd found a set of GitHub repositories that were scanning for apps vulnerable to React2Shell (CVE-2025-55182) and the Next.js middleware authorization bypass (CVE-2025-29927), and trying to exploit them.She'd uncovered 38 of these repos on her own and determined they had targeted more than 20,000 hosts and compromised about 277 of them, and that some of the repos contained stolen data sitting in plaintext. She asked for a review of her research since OpenSourceMalware is a dedicated source for GitHub threats. Our analysis shows that this is an end-to-end automated hacking framework built on GitHub Actions. Domains go in and stolen credentials come out. We're calling the campaign React2STEAL, after the React2Shell flaw it exploits and what it does once it's in. See all the threat records under the react2steal tagOur findings confirmed her discoveries and expanded the scope:We confirmed Karina's discovery: These repos are attack infrastructure, not a malicious Action that someone would install. They host an infostealer and the exploit scripts that deliver it, and they double as the drop site for what it steals, which makes them malicious repositories even though nobody downloads them. Each holds its own GitHub Actions workflow that uses GitHub's runners to scan for Next.js servers and attempt to exploit known CVEs (React2Shell and CVE-2025-29927) against them. When an exploit works, it runs a credential-stealing script on the victim's server that grabs environment variables, cloud credentials and API keys, and the workflow commits what it took back into the same public repo.We expanded the dataset: In total we found 45 React2STEAL repos, set up in three waves since October 22. They were still committing new results about every 11 minutes when we published this analysis. Those results list at least 1,281 victim hostnames across about 1,100 domains. In a single repo, the target lists alone hold about 18 million unique hostnames. The result files hold process environment dumps, and the credentials that show up most often are database URLs, Stripe keys and AI provider keys. We also found that the payload steals full config files and the server's AWS credentials, and that the stolen records are strong evidence that it actually ran on those servers.We pushed the timeline back: Dated comments the author left in the code suggest the pipeline was running at volume from at least September 10, about six weeks before the first React2STEAL repos were created on October 22.We found a connection to another campaign: wfx-loot is a separate campaign, running since November 10, that uses thousands of hijacked GitHub accounts to steal CI secrets. Most of the React2STEAL repos carry the probe file wfx-loot pushes before it plants its stealer, and most React2STEAL owners have wfx-loot probe pull requests on their repos.What we don't know (yet) is who runs React2STEAL, how the account tokens were obtained, or whether one operator used them for both attacks. The evidence shows that the GitHub accounts running React2STEAL were also used in wfx-loot.TL;DRCampaign: React2STEAL, in GitHub repos named ci-wk-<number>Threat actor: Unknown. The GitHub account dascxzcw is our best lead.Targets: React and Next.js servers vulnerable to React2Shell (CVE-2025-55182) and CVE-2025-29927Infrastructure: 45 repos on victims' GitHub accounts, each running the attack through GitHub ActionsStolen data: Environment variables, .env and config files, AWS role credentials and AI provider keys, which it tests with live requestsExfiltration: Committed to the same public repos. A Telegram channel is built in but off by default.Scale: At least 1,281 victim hostnames. One repo's target lists alone hold about 18 million unique hosts.Timeline: Repos created from October 22, with dated code comments going back to September 10Related campaign: Many of the same accounts were also used […]

title: Official Microsoft agent-framework PyPI package compromised
text:
The OpenSourceMalware team discovered two malicious releases of Microsoft's agent-framework package on PyPI, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2. Both add a credential stealer that runs automatically whenever Python starts in the affected environment, without anyone importing the package.See the threat report here. This isn't a typosquat. The releases came from the legitimate Microsoft-associated PyPI publisher, so trust in the project name, the publisher, lock files or earlier clean releases wouldn't have protected anyone who resolved either version. PyPI has quarantined the publisher, but the threat actor is still believed to have publishing access. It's a reminder that trusted publisher access and Python .pth files both deserve attention. A one-line startup file shipped under an established package name runs before the application's own code and inherits every credential on the developer workstation or CI runner.The stealer searches environment variables, credential files and other processes' environments for secrets. Then it goes further and requests fresh GitHub Actions, Azure DevOps and Azure managed identity tokens, and sends everything to a webhook.site URL hidden in the source as Base64. That combination of passive theft and active token requests makes it especially dangerous in cloud build environments, because even short-lived tokens are useful when they're exfiltrated right away.Treat any installation of 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 as a credential compromise, even if the publisher is restored or a newer version is released.TL;DRThreat type: Supply chain credential stealerEcosystem: PyPIMalicious versions: agent-framework 1.26.1 and 1.26.2Impact: Theft of developer credentials, CI/CD tokens, cloud identity tokens, application secrets and registry credentialsExecution: A .pth file runs the stealer during ordinary Python startup, with no import of the package requiredExfiltration: Compressed, Base64-encoded data sent by HTTPS POST to a dedicated webhook.site URLRegistry action: PyPI quarantined the Microsoft publisher because unauthorized publishing access is believed to remain activeWhat's in the packageThe unpacked 1.26.2 distribution looks plausible at first glance. Its metadata names Microsoft as the author, links to the legitimate Agent Framework project and includes the expected project documentation. The contents tell a different story. Alongside a metadata helper module, it contains two unexpected files:af_runtime_diag.pth
af_runtime_diag.py
agent_framework_meta/__init__.py
agent_framework-1.26.2.dist-info/The names suggest harmless runtime diagnostics. Static analysis shows they collect and exfiltrate credentials instead.Version 1.26.1 is also confirmed malicious, but the hashes and line-level behavior below refer to the 1.26.2 artifact unless stated otherwise.Publisher compromise and quarantineThe malicious releases were published through Microsoft's official PyPI publisher account. The threat actor is believed to still have publishing access because 1.26.2 was published after PyPI quarantined 1.26.1.Public download statistics for agent-framework show demand for the project as a whole, but they don't say how many times 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 were installed. Don't read those figures as a count of victims or of downloads of the malicious versions.Technical analysisAutomatic execution through a .pth fileThe attack starts with a 23-byte file named af_runtime_diag.pth that contains one line:import af_runtime_diagPython's site initialization runs executable import lines in .pth files. Once this file is in site-packages, af_runtime_diag loads during normal interpreter startup. The victim doesn't need to import agent_framework or call any malicious function.At the bottom of af_runtime_diag.py, the module calls _start() immediately. That sets _AF_TEL=1 to stop it running twice, then tries to run the collector in a detached forked child. If fork() is unavailable or fails, it falls back to a daemon thread. Broad exception handlers suppress […]

title: Versioned Gmail Addresses Link Four Malicious npm Packages

They're named that way because it's their consistent handle across GitHub and numerous online platforms.litecore-lib-ltc is a working Litecoin wallet library first published to npm on March 1, 2026. title: MITRE Acknowledges Inaccurate Publication Timestamps in 87% of Its Recent CVE Records
text: BackSecurity NewsMITRE Acknowledges Inaccurate Publication Timestamps in 87% of Its Recent CVE RecordsMITRE acknowledges inaccurate publication timestamps in 87% of its recent CVE records and plans to retire the legacy system responsible in 2027.Sarah GoodingNov 18, 2026|4 min read MITRE has acknowledged that a legacy publishing system is responsible for inaccurate timestamps in thousands of CVE records, following research showing that 87% of the organization's CVEs published over the past year were assigned a publication time of exactly midnight UTC. MITRE says the legacy system responsible for the problem will be phased out in the first quarter of 2027.The findings come from security researcher Jerry Gamblin, founder of RogoLabs, an independent open source research lab focused on vulnerability intelligence. His projects include the CNA Scorecard, which evaluates the completeness of CVE records, and CNAPulse, which tracks vulnerability publishing activity across CVE Numbering Authorities (CNAs). Socket has previously covered both projects and Gamblin's broader research into CVE data quality.Analyzing CVE records published over the 52 weeks ending November 16, 2026, Gamblin found that 3,901 of MITRE's 4,509 CVEs (87%) had a datePublished timestamp of exactly 00:00:00.000Z. Across the other 425 CNAs, none of the 100,235 records carried that same timestamp.The distribution creates the appearance that MITRE publishes hundreds of vulnerability records at precisely midnight on weekdays. In reality, those timestamps do not represent the actual time the records were published. The CVE Record Format defines datePublished as the date and time a CVE record was first published in the CVE List. Researchers and automated systems can use that field to track publication activity, measure delays, and analyze vulnerability reporting trends.Gamblin first raised the issue on GitHub in July, calling for changes to CVE publication requirements and more accurate timestamps.To confirm the discrepancy, he compared recorded publication timestamps with the first appearance of each CVE in the official CVE List's cves/deltaLog.json change log.For 202 MITRE records published between October 19 and November 16, he found that 144 records stamped at midnight UTC had a median delay of 15.8 hours between their recorded publication time and their first appearance in the change log. The remaining 58 MITRE records, which carried other publication times, appeared a median of 4.6 minutes after their recorded timestamps. Records from other CNAs showed a comparable median delay of 4.5 minutes.The comparison provides evidence that the midnight timestamps are placeholders rather than actual publication times. Gamblin also found that the dates themselves were accurate in the sample he examined.“Timestamps are one of the few fields in a CVE Record that are supposed to be objective and machine-trustworthy," Gamblin wrote in his issue on GitHub in July. "Right now, the largest single source of CVE Records is still shipping fabricated timestamps on 84% of what it published in the last 30 days, while every other CNA in the sample gets this right at 0%. Anything downstream that measures time-to-publish, time-to-update, or disclosure latency (EPSS, CNA scorecards, research like mine) is quietly built on bad data for the biggest chunk of the dataset."Researchers tracking CVE publication delays could interpret the 15.8-hour gap as evidence that MITRE takes much longer than other CNAs to make records available. But because the midnight timestamps are artificial, that gap cannot reliably measure publication delays. The date may still be useful for daily reporting, but the timestamp cannot reliably establish when during that day a CVE record became available."For me the problem is uniformity more than precision," Gamblin wrote. "What breaks things is one field that means two different things depending on who published the record." Responding to Gamblin's findings on LinkedIn, Alec […]

FBI: Cybercrime Takedowns Need Hyperscaler Help to Hit Home
FBI Cybercrime Takedowns Need Backing From Tech Giants to Have Any Lasting Impact

Shaun Waterman •
November 18, 2026

$('.fa.fa-print').click(function () {
window.print();
});

Image: Shutterstock

AUSTIN, TEXAS - Unilateral FBI operations against cybercrime groups and other online threat actors have only "ephemeral" effects, the bureau's top cyber agent said Tuesday. To have lasting impact, operations must involve internet infrastructure giants, cloud hyperscalers or ecosystem owners, Assistant Director of the FBI Cyber Division Brett Leatherman told the Billington Critical Infrastructure Summit.See Also: A Darkening Landscape: AI, Friend and Foe of Cyber Resilience
Closer partnership with tech giants is a pillar of the FBI's first-ever public cybercrime strategy, published earlier this year. The strategy also calls for the FBI to work more closely with the victims of cyberattacks.
There are a small number of "partners out there who can actually conduct operations on their own infrastructure," Leatherman said, "Think the major cloud providers, the major endpoint or operating system providers, those who can conduct effects against actors … at the same time the FBI conducts effects against their command and control infrastructure upstream."
These coordinated strikes against cyber threat actors are called "joint sequenced operations," Leatherman said. "If we take down their infrastructure that they're using for command and control—and at the same time Microsoft or Google or somebody like that is conducting terms of service violations or moving that capability across Azure or AWS or other environments—we can have an outsized impact against the actors."
Without the infrastructure owners' cooperation, taking down command and control is only a temporary victory, since threat actors can quickly rebuild or buy in new infrastructure.
"When we do it alone, it is more of an ephemeral operation," Leatherman said. "It's more temporary, and so we want that sustained impact, and working with those operational partners is increasingly important to us."
The new strategy calls for stepping up joint sequenced operations, leveraging the capabilities of tech hyperscalers and other digital infrastructure owners and operators to impose lasting costs on cybercrime actors.
"We have conducted over 100 joint sequenced operations over the last 18 months," said Leatherman, adding that "deterrence means scaling our work through our partnerships."
The strategy was also bearing fruit when it came to personal criminal accountability, Leatherman said: "In the last 18 months, almost 600 individuals were charged and arrested by the FBI as a result of their cyber activity."
Leatherman also emphasized the critical importance of victim companies coming forward: "None of the joint sequenced operations that we've done over the last few years have been done without victims or organizations coming to the FBI and engaging with us, and enabling us to move quickly against the threat, so victim reporting is incredibly important."

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman on Sept. 25, 2026 during a public appearance in Kolkata, India. (Image: Shutterstock)

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said that while he wishes the Hugging Face incident hadn't happened, the company had no way of knowing how unsafe the agents were.See Also: 43% Are Piloting Healthcare AI Agents. Just 3% Have Deployed Them

Speaking at the New York Times' DealBook Summit, Altman and OpenAI president Greg Brockman spoke about how the company is navigating what they see as a "newly challenging" period.

Altman said the company has always followed an iterative deployment approach, releasing new models to smaller groups and adjusting things before allowing wider access.

"We wish Hugging Face hadn't happened," Altman said. "The only way that we have known how to make this technology safe is to confront reality."

OpenAI agents coordinated to hack into Hugging Face's model repository system. The incident fueled the current AI safety debates and put focus on agent behavior. Both OpenAI and Anthropic paused training of their newer models so they could upgrade their safety guardrails and misalignment evaluations.

Altman is one of the AI executives who expressed support and urged the industry to "pace" AI model development. Slowing down AI innovation has become a controversial topic in the AI world, with some leaders arguing that slowing down will erode the United States' competitive advantage.

"We're not going to make everybody happy," Altman said. "If we talk too much about taking extra care for safety or there are risks that we really need coordination to mitigate, people are going to accuse us of regulatory capture or trying to slow down innovation."

He added that if OpenAI thinks the opposite, "people will say don't kill us all, a very reasonable thing." Altman said the company will continue to do what it believes "will actually deliver a safe future with people in control."

How Recent IT Outages Expose Risks of AI-Driven Patch Rush
Experts Warn That Accelerated Remediation Can Destabilize Aging Infrastructure

Tiffany Wang •
November 18, 2026

$('.fa.fa-print').click(function () {
window.print();
});

Image: Shutterstock

Pressure to patch vulnerabilities at machine speed can leave organizations shooting themselves in the foot - as the globe witnessed for itself over roughly a week of digital outages.See Also: Frictionless Security: How AI is Redefining Access in Highly Regulated Industries
A growing consensus among industry and government is that, rather than artificial intelligence agents or AI-powered attacks being responsible for a days-long binge of systems collapse, it was fear of those threats that caused the outages, through forced upgrades and patches onto decades-old systems.

"Organizations are facing a balancing act," said Dan Schiappa, president of technology and services at threat intelligence firm Arctic Wolf. "Security vulnerabilities that are actively being exploited often require rapid remediation because a security incident can have far greater consequences than an IT disruption. At the same time, patches should be rolled out in a phased manner so teams can monitor their behavior, validate effectiveness, and identify unintended impacts before broader deployment," Schiappa told ISMG.

The patching fever began when Anthropic released Claude Mythos Preview in April, a powerful frontier model promising autonomous discovery of thousands of zero-days (see: Anthropic Calls Its New Model Too Dangerous to Release).
Taking Mozilla as an example, developers behind the Firefox web browser patched fewer than 30 bugs every month in 2025 - but shipped over 400 fixes in April this year. Most of those flaws were identified by Claude Mythos Preview.

For a big technology provider like Microsoft, the bug explosion happened on an even larger scale. The company's monthly security update, known as Patch Tuesday, grew from fewer than 100 fixes before April to patches for more than 1,000 vulnerabilities in the past two months.

Through Project Glasswing, major technology vendors were given a short period of time to sample test Mythos and patch their vulnerabilities before the advanced capabilities became public. Six months later, Anthropic expanded access to Mythos through its Cyber Verification Program, allowing qualifying cybersecurity professionals to apply for tools ranging from malware reverse-engineering to penetration testing.

A similar circumstance unfolded at OpenAI, where the company launched its Daybreak program in May to give select enterprises offensive cyber models. It then broadened the program into two capability tiers for more defenders to participate in August.

At the same time, open-weight models advanced rapidly, putting capabilities comparable to those of frontier models into the hands of anyone interested, without the same guardrails. It meant bug hunters with little experience were digging up serious vulnerabilities.

Vendors couldn't keep up with the amount of bugs AI was finding - many open source projects shut down or paused their bug bounty programs in response - and researchers were complaining about having to wait forever to hear back from a company whose bug they reported.

Project Zero, a team of security researchers at Google who study zero-days, recently upended its long-running vulnerability disclosure policy. Fearing that researchers or hackers will disclose or use the flaws before patches are rolled out, the team is shortening its disclosure timeline from 120 days to 90 and will reduce that to 30 days by 2028.
Despite the discovery frenzy, few of the bugs found using AI were actually exploited. Patrick Garrity, a security researcher at VulnCheck, has been pooling […]

Blame Culture Is Making Cybersecurity's Talent Problem Worse
Punitive Security Pushes Employees to Hide Mistakes, Practitioners to Avoid Risk

Gilles Castro

•
November 18, 2026

$('.fa.fa-print').click(function () {
window.print();
});

Image: Shutterstock
Security leaders have spent years warning employees not to click phishing links, reuse passwords or send sensitive data to unapproved tools. When someone does it anyway and an incident ensues, the hunt for the person responsible begins almost immediately.See Also: Why Banks Are Rethinking Fraud and Cybersecurity Together
That finger-pointing instinct may be making cybersecurity's talent problem even worse.
A culture built around punishment gives employees a reason to hide mistakes. It also gives security practitioners a reason to protect themselves instead of taking the risks required to improve defenses.
Organizations have spent too much time treating individual failures as the cause of security incidents while paying too little attention to the controls, policies and business decisions surrounding them.
Historically, what we would do is just blame the end user for their failures. Security teams even have a colloquial term for it - "blaming the wetware."
The problem extends beyond end users. Security practitioners face even higher stakes when an incident occurs on their watch. The end user may have to worry about taking the blame, but security professionals could get fired and lose their livelihood.
Blame culture really matters when it comes to recruiting and retention. Organizations say they need cybersecurity professionals who can challenge assumptions, experiment, learn from failure and work closely with employees across the business. But a workplace in which mistakes threaten careers encourages the opposite behavior.
Practitioners learn to minimize personal exposure. Employees learn to keep quiet. Security becomes an enforcement function rather than a partner to the business.
Fear Creates the Wrong Incentives
Phishing offers one of the clearest examples.
An employee who clicks a simulated phishing message can be shamed or punished for failing the test. But punishment doesn't necessarily stop the next click. It may instead make the employee less willing to report it.
That creates an obvious security problem. Early reporting can give defenders valuable time to reset credentials, isolate systems and investigate activity before an attacker moves further through the environment.
The same dynamic affects security teams. If practitioners expect an incident to cost them their jobs, they have an incentive to avoid decisions that create personal risk. And that can lead to a risk-averse culture.
Risk aversion may feel safer, but it can create new weaknesses. Security teams can make controls so restrictive that employees look for workarounds to get their jobs done.
Unsanctioned artificial intelligence tools are an emerging example. An organization may approve one enterprise platform while employees turn to personal accounts for other AI services because those tools are a better fit for their work.
The security failure isn't simply that an employee broke a rule. Leaders also need to ask why the approved environment failed to meet the employee's business need.
Blame Makes a Hard Job Even Harder to Sell
The cybersecurity profession already asks a great deal of its practitioners. They must make decisions with incomplete information, respond quickly during incidents and defend organizations against adversaries who only need one opening.
In a culture where one mistake can end a career, cybersecurity jobs will be less attractive and harder to retain.
That becomes especially damaging as security programs try to widen their talent pools. Organizations need people with different professional backgrounds, technical skills and ways of […]

The Week the Patches Bit Back
Washington Says Outages Were Not an Attack and That Should Worry CIOs More

Jennifer Lawinski

•
November 18, 2026

$('.fa.fa-print').click(function () {
window.print();
});

Image: Shutterstock
If you were writing a disaster movie, they'd make you cut something out.See Also: Why Banks Are Rethinking Fraud and Cybersecurity Together

It would seem too implausible.

Microsoft 365 went down on Thursday. By Friday night, the FAA had grounded flights nationwide. On Monday, a software bug at JPMorgan Chase froze transfers and ATMs and dragged Zelle and other banks down with it. Apple, United Airlines and the National Security Agency's classified network had all suffered outages by Tuesday evening.

Six outages big enough to hit the news in less than a week.

Here's where the hero sweeps in, right?

But this tale has neither heroes nor villains, and while Washington has said these outages are not part of a coordinated cyberattack, that's not necessarily comforting news. Sometimes it's the story without a real bad guy that's the scariest.

"Lots of institutions, because these vulnerabilities have been identified, are patching. They're taking their systems down, they're upgrading them, they're putting patches in place. And as they upgrade them, they're not coming back as expected in all cases," said Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton on Tuesday.

He said the government found no sign of coordination or state sponsorship.

Palo Alto Networks CEO Nikesh Arora argued on X Tuesday that the week's events were no coincidence. "AI is making it easy for hackers to attack multiple customers. All incident responders are busy, unfortunately there is no silver bullet," he wrote.

Arora added that IT teams are flooded with patches from vendors, creating a deluge. "Although all well-intentioned, vendors who are finding vulnerabilities are patching them and pushing them to customers as soon as they can. The challenge: IT teams are overwhelmed with goodness!"

Apparently vendors are killing their customers with kindness, and the patch tsunami that some feared when Anthropic unveiled Mythos - an AI model that found thousands of software flaws - to a limited group of defenders in April, is starting to hit.

AI-driven bug hunting has tech teams now managing an unprecedented number of fixes every month - or more. Microsoft's July and August Patch Tuesdays, at 622 and 419 fixes, were the largest in the program's history, and Microsoft credited AI-assisted discovery. Google's threat analysts say disclosed vulnerabilities doubled this year. Last month a PHP flaw found with AI's help sent website operators scrambling, and Clayton tied the NSA outage to patches for it.

Mythos brought worries that attackers would soon have the upper hand, able to exploit flaws that AI models discovered at machine speed, but it has, in practice, also given the defenders a real headache as they juggle thousands of fixes jammed into systems never built to change this quickly.

Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince warned last month that for a couple of years, every week would "feel like the sky is falling."

So far, that prediction is aging well.

The FAA blamed a router upgrade that flooded a legacy network with connection attempts. Microsoft traced its outage to a July bug that lay dormant until heavy traffic woke it. Apple pointed to "an internal update."

Combine aging infrastructure, legacy systems and understaffed teams. The calls were coming from inside the house.

"We are now entirely dependent on systems that almost nobody understands end to end, that increasingly few people can triage, and that attackers can now probe at machine speed - just as the cavalry disappears," Nicole Perlroth, a venture capitalist and former cybersecurity journalist, wrote Tuesday […]

Organizations need more computing resources as artificial intelligence agents execute longer-running tasks and operate with greater autonomy, said Nvidia following the resignation of founding CEO Jensen Huang.See Also: Webinar | Closing Visibility Gaps. How Leading Organizations Are Securing and Scaling Their Cloud-First Architecture
The Silicon Valley-based chip giant said agentic AI is a major driver of computing demand, with weekly token volume on OpenRouter increasing 35-fold year-over-year as agentic workloads account for some 80% of tokens. Nvidia told investors Tuesday its new security capabilities restrict agent access to files and tools, monitor agent behavior and enforce restrictions in milliseconds.

Nvidia's leadership spoke with investors just five days after Huang resigned after disclosing personal behavior inconsistent with the company's code of conduct. Sustaining Infrastructure Demand Beyond 2027
Jones said Nvidia's board will consider internal and external candidates for the permanent CEO position, and will prioritize leadership capabilities suited to an industry shaped by national security and advanced semiconductor technologies. Nvidia also established a committee to strengthen its engagement with U.S. government agencies and its oversight of national security and export control matters.
"While this was an unexpected transition, the board acted deliberately and in the best interest of the company's employees, customers, partners and shareholders," Jones said.
Declining inference costs are encouraging greater AI adoption, creating more demand for computing resources. Token prices have fallen nearly 60% since May, but GPU rental prices continue to increase because demand is outpacing available capacity. Hopper GPUs have been recontracted at up to twice their original prices under multiyear agreements, while B300 rental rates have increased over 60%.
"Nvidia compute remains fully utilized across every hyperscaler and neocloud we serve, underscoring the productivity, durability and fungibility of our infrastructure," Kress said.

Nvidia expects CPU revenue to more than double in fiscal 2028.

title: Outage or attack? Don’t let social media fill in the gaps
GTA 6 scams could cost you your account, money, or crypto
text: In this articleFake GTA 6 promotions, codes, apps, and merch are targeting playersSome sites mimic Google sign-in pages or ask visitors to connect crypto walletsHow to avoid the scams and what to do if you’ve already interacted with oneScammers are using GTA 6’s launch hype to promote fake free-game offers, pre-order codes, discounted keys, and map downloads. The lures can lead to sponsored offers, fake sign-in pages, dubious downloads, or payment and wallet traps.We also found sites offering fake Android downloads, promoting crypto tokens, asking visitors to connect crypto wallets, and selling unofficial merchandise with an AI-generated product image. Some try to steal account details; others aim to earn commissions from clicks and sign-ups, take payment, or get visitors to approve risky wallet requests.Here’s what we found and how to spot these lures.Why GTA 6 is such a big dealGTA V came out in 2013, and Take-Two says it has sold more than 230 million copies worldwide. The first GTA VI trailer drew more than 90 million YouTube views in its first 24 hours, earning a Guinness World Record, while the second trailer received more than 475 million views across platforms in its first 24 hours.Pre-orders set records on the PlayStation Store and the Microsoft Store, and Take-Two says demand reached “unprecedented levels”. The standard edition costs $79.99 in the US, while the Ultimate Edition is $99.99.That’s a huge audience, a long wait, and a high price. It gives scammers a ready-made reason to promise free access, cheap keys, and other shortcuts.A free GTA 6 that costs you your Google accountThe first site keeps it simple: “Get GTA VI for free.” There’s no prize draw, the page promises. Everyone who meets the promotion terms gets the game.A fake promotion page offering GTA VI to “everyone who meets the promotion terms”Click Get the game and you’re asked to choose PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S, or PC. Then comes the real ask: sign in with Google “to complete verification.” An activation code will supposedly arrive at the email address linked to your Google account.The “verification” step asks visitors to sign in with GoogleThe Continue with Google button doesn’t open Google. It reloads the same scam site with a random ID in the address and shows a convincing copy of Google’s sign-in page. The browser tab even reads “Sign in – Google Accounts.” The giveaway is the address bar, which still shows the scam domain.A fake Google sign-in page hosted on the scam siteThe site puts a lot of effort into looking legitimate. It has pages of “promotion terms” and FAQs about eligibility, age requirements, and a “separate phase” for PC. One answer reassures visitors that the landing page has no email, password, or payment fields.Technically, that’s true. Those fields are one click away, on the fake Google page.A Google account is rarely just email. It may also be the key to your YouTube channel, Google Drive, saved passwords, and other services where you’ve used “Sign in with Google.” Gaming accounts linked to that email address may be reset through it too.There is no free GTA 6 promotion on this site. Don’t enter your Google password on a page hosted by an unrelated website.“Free pre-order codes” that end in sponsored offersThe most common lure we found was the free code generator. These sites promise a working GTA VI redeem or access code for PS5 or Xbox, usually after a few “steps.”A “Limited Access Program” promising complimentary GTA VI access codesThe site above spells out those steps. Visitors are told to open the page in their default browser—a hint that traffic may arrive from social media apps—complete a “short 2-minute questionnaire,” and “finish the required sponsored offers to complete qualification.” Only then will they supposedly receive “final instructions” for getting a code.Behind the scenes, the page looks up the visitor’s location and sends them to affiliate tracking links tagged with the site’s name. title: Russian national indicted for allegedly acting as a foreign agent targeting Silicon Valley tech and defense firm
text:
SAN FRANCISCO – A federal grand jury has indicted Igor D’iu, a Russian national, on charges of conspiring to act as an agent of a foreign government, acting as an agent of a foreign government without notice to the Attorney General, interstate stalking, and fraud in connection with identification documents, all in connection with an alleged scheme to conduct surveillance and gather information about employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company.
“The allegations in this case describe a state-sponsored operation to target and harass employees of an American technology and defense company because of that company’s assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia,” said United States Attorney Craig H. Missakian. “We will not tolerate any efforts – by foreign governments or otherwise – to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations.  And my office, working in concert with our law enforcement partners, will aggressively pursue and prosecute those who seek to carry out such illegal operations on American soil.”
“The charges announced today underscore the FBI’s commitment to protecting people and businesses in the United States from foreign governments that seek to intimidate, surveil, harass, or otherwise exert control beyond their own borders,” said FBI Special Agent in Charge Scott R. Schelble.  “As alleged, this case demonstrates that such conduct can extend beyond traditional political targets and reach into the private sector, targeting employees because of the organizations they represent and the interests they advance.  We are grateful to our local law enforcement partners at the Palo Alto Police Department and the San Francisco Police Department, whose initial information helped bring this matter to the FBI’s attention.  The FBI will continue working with our partners to identify, investigate, and disrupt foreign government efforts to threaten, silence, or intimidate people and companies on U.S. soil.”

The affidavit and indictment allege that D’iu traveled from Istanbul, Turkey, to Mexico City in June 2026, where his co-conspirators connected him with an individual who helped him cross the United States and Mexico border.  After D’iu entered the United States, co-conspirators allegedly instructed D’iu to purchase laptops, cell phones, wireless networking equipment, and remote access software, all of which he did, to facilitate his assignments.  According to the affidavit, D’iu’s co-conspirators directed him to visit a coffee shop near the company’s Palo Alto office, identify company employees, and photograph their laptop screens while they worked.  His co-conspirators also allegedly instructed him to position his laptop at designated locations near the company so they could remotely access it and attempt to collect information from company employees in the vicinity.

title: Uber says hackers used a stolen login at one of its AI vendors to take driver's licence images and ID details of 149,346 people. Source: https://www.securityweek.com/uber-data-breach-impacts-150000-people/ #hYYa #Privacy #DataBreach #InfoSec
text:
Uber is notifying roughly 150,000 drivers that their personal information was stolen in a data breach involving a third-party services provider.

The company learned of the incident on October 9 and immediately severed its data connections with the provider and launched an investigation.

On October 13, the investigation determined that the hackers used compromised service provider credentials on October 7 to access data Uber had shared with the provider.

According to Uber, the hackers accessed images of driver’s licenses and personal information such as names, addresses, dates of birth, driver’s license numbers, and government-issued ID numbers.

The company says that the data was stored in an environment created and managed by Uber’s Cloud Security team. While alerts were enabled, none were triggered because the threat actor used valid credentials.

“The service provider’s compromised credentials did not provide access to other Uber systems. The investigation remains ongoing,” the company said.

Uber has filed data breach notifications with multiple US states, including California, Iowa, Massachusetts, South Carolina, Texas, and Vermont, and reportedly notified the Texas Attorney General’s Office that a total of 149,346 people were affected.

Uber is providing the potentially affected individuals with free credit monitoring and fraud assistance services.

Uber did not identify the service provider in its breach notifications, but a company spokesperson confirmed to TechCrunch that the incident involved Fireworks AI, a cloud platform for running and fine-tuning open source AI models.

Fireworks initially said it had found no evidence that customer personal information, models or datasets had been accessed. However, in a November 9 update, the company acknowledged that the breach also affected account and billing information, as well as some customer datasets and incomplete models.

SecurityWeek has emailed Uber for additional information on the data breach and will update this article if the company responds.

Nov. 18, 2026 — Data breaches at external service providers exposed employee data at DHL Group and customer information at Office Partner. Payment details were reportedly not affected. Both firms say vulnerabilities are fixed; customers should change reused passwords and watch for phishing. 🔐🚨 www.heise.de/en/news/Data-breaches-hit-Office-Partner-and-DHL-Group-11529577.html #Cybersecurity #DataBreach
text: Attackers breached IT systems at external service providers used by both DHL Group and Office Partner GmbH, and copied sensitive data. Both companies have notified those affected. At DHL Group, the attackers broke into a service provider responsible for internal surveys. They reportedly downloaded selected employee records belonging to DHL Group staff. In an email to employees, the company says the data included names, ages, business email addresses, selected personal email addresses and organizational information. However, information such as passwords, tax, salary or bank details was not affected. The external service provider has since fixed the vulnerability. DHL Group is working closely with the relevant authorities to investigate the incident. According to a notice from Turkey’s data protection authority, the KVKK, 10,622 employees in Turkey alone were affected by the incident on Nov. 2 of this year. DHL Group has about 584,000 employees, while Office Partner GmbH says it has more than 1 million customers. Apparently, some of their data was stored by an external service provider, which unauthorized individuals accessed. In an email to customers, Office Partner says its core systems and online stores were not affected. The data stolen from the service provider reportedly included names, billing and shipping addresses, phone numbers, invoices, email addresses for user accounts and encrypted passwords. At least payment and credit card details were not among the data. The unauthorized individuals had access as early as Nov. 7. The company says it has no indication so far that the data has been misused. However, customers should change their Office Partner password, as well as on any other platforms where they used the same password. As with DHL, the security vulnerability has been fixed; Office Partner has also filed a criminal complaint and notified the data protection authority. Criminals can use the copied data to send more convincing phishing emails in particular. DHL Group employees and Office Partner customers should therefore stay alert when they receive messages. Office Partner recommends checking the sender’s authenticity and not sharing any information if anything seems suspicious. Such cyberattacks remain commonplace. In early November, attackers, for example, breached web host Mittwald through the MCP server; in a second wave of attacks, the provider’s website was also affected. Access to the customer systems’ management interface and SSH was severely restricted. (dmk) Don't miss any news – follow us on Facebook, LinkedIn or Mastodon.
